What happens with the tax when a Darke County house sells?

Before the deed reaches the recorder, the buyer files a conveyance fee statement with the auditor on form DTE 100, or DTE 100EX when an exemption applies. The seller pays the conveyance fee and any county transfer tax at that point, and the auditor stamps the deed.

The statement also asks about homestead and farmland. Where the property carried a homestead or owner-occupancy reduction, the two sides sign a sworn instrument that deals with how that reduction ends, and farmland that was under agricultural valuation gets its own statement on form DTE 102. The auditor's conveyance fee calculator adds the parcel transfer fee to the total.

If any tax is delinquent, get a payoff figure from the treasurer so the title company can fold it into the closing numbers.

More questions about Darke County, OH Property Tax Guide

Which office issues a Darke County tax bill?

The treasurer, at 937-547-7365. The auditor's real estate division, at 937-547-7308, answers questions about the value behind the bill.

What is the last day to contest a Darke County value?

March 31 of the following tax year, unless first-half collection closes later. The DTE 1 goes to the auditor.

Does Darke County have a tax credit for older owners?

Yes. The Ohio homestead program covers owners aged 65 or older, disabled owners and qualifying surviving spouses. Apply on DTE 105A and ask the auditor which income limit applies.

Is a sale possible with tax still owed in Darke County?

Yes. Get a payoff figure from the treasurer, and use the auditor's delinquency report to see what is posted against the parcel.

How do I find the rate for my Darke County parcel?

Try the tax estimator on the real estate website or the yearly rate pages in the auditor's forms list, and confirm your taxing district by phone.

Delaware County by the numbers

Which Delaware County offices deal with a property tax bill?

Two elected offices in one Delaware building divide the work. The auditor appraises property and administers credits, while the treasurer mails bills and takes payment. You can reach both on the first floor of 145 N. Union St., Delaware, OH 43015, on weekdays.

The recorder files deeds from that same address, and a three-member Board of Revision hears value complaints. If you owe tax, the treasurer is your contact for the balance, and the auditor is your contact for value questions or credits.

What does Delaware County look like before a sale?

Delaware County grew from 174,214 people in 2010 to a 2020 census count of 214,124, and the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 242,032, with 95,340 housing units. Land area is 443 square miles. The Olentangy River, Alum Creek and the Scioto drain it from north to south, and the county borders Franklin County on its southern edge, according to Wikipedia.

QuickFacts reports a typical owner-occupied home value of $445,500 for 2020 to 2024 and household income at the midpoint of $133,540. Owner-occupancy runs 78.5%. Builders pulled 2,016 permits in 2025, so a resale listing competes with a steady flow of new houses.

Towns inside the county include the city of Delaware (the seat), Powell, Sunbury, and parts of Dublin and Westerville, plus the villages of Ashley, Galena, Ostrander and Shawnee Hills. Which school district a house sits in changes the bill. A June 2026 treasurer notice names Dublin, Westerville and Olentangy as districts where residential parcels were left out of the new inflation cap credit.

What are the Delaware County property tax due dates?

Bills come due twice a year. The treasurer's home page gives February 10, 2027 for the first installment and July 12, 2027 for the second, on the tax year 2026 bills. Because billing runs a year behind, the 2025 tax year bills were the ones collected in 2026.

  • The 2025 second-half deadline was moved from July 10 to August 17, 2026, because House Bill 186 had to be applied to the bills first.
  • The treasurer's June 2026 notice says the extension applied to 2026 only and that collections go back to the February 10 and July 10 pattern.
  • Forms on the treasurer's site include the 2 1/2% reduction, escrow or ACH automatic deduction, homestead, penalty remission, property valuation complaint and a tax mailing address change.
  • Past payments appear on the auditor's parcel record: open the Tax tab and scroll to the bottom of the Tax Detail screen.

For a question about one bill, phone the treasurer on (740) 833-2480.

What did House Bill 186 change on Delaware County bills?

House Bill 186 created an Inflation Cap Credit that lowers taxes on certain school district levies, and the credit was applied retroactively to tax year 2025 for real property. According to the treasurer's announcement, residential and agricultural parcels receive it everywhere in the county except in the Dublin, Westerville and Olentangy school districts.

Owners who qualified and had already paid in full see any overpayment applied to the following tax year. The credit shows as its own line on the second-half bill and on the property record at the auditor's site. The treasurer also posted a summary of the bill on its home page. A seller preparing a listing should pull the parcel's tax detail from the auditor's site rather than quote an old bill to a buyer.

How do I contest my value with the Delaware County Board of Revision?

Send a formal complaint to the auditor during the window that opens January 2 and closes March 31. The board looks at what the property was worth on the January 1 lien date, and its page says it will not take complaints about the tax rate or the taxes. The statute, Ohio Revised Code 5715.19, sets the deadline at March 31 or the end of first-half collection, whichever comes later.

The auditor's 2026 Triennial Valuation Update page says the informal review window has ended and names March 31, 2027 as the last day for a formal complaint against the value as of January 1, 2027. Complaints can be handed in or mailed to 145 N. Union St., emailed to auditor@co.delaware.oh.us, or faxed to (740) 833-2899.

  • Helpful attachments, per the board, are a recent independent appraisal, photos of damage, comparable sales, and the closing statement and purchase contract if the home just sold.
  • Hearings run like a short court session, with sworn witnesses and marked exhibits, and usually take 10 to 20 minutes.
  • Decisions sit for 30 days before values change. An owner who still disagrees can go to the Ohio Board of Tax Appeals or the county Court of Common Pleas, with 30 days counted from the date on the decision letter.
  • The board will not cut a value just because the auditor's figures for neighbors look lower, when those neighbors had no arm's length sale.

Which tax relief programs matter if I sell in Delaware County?

The homestead exemption is the big one, and it follows the owner instead of the house. The auditor's page describes a cut equal to the tax on $25,000 of market value, for owners aged 65 and up or anyone permanently and totally disabled, covering a home plus up to one acre. First-time applicants must pass an income test. A person who got the credit for tax year 2013 is exempt from that test and carries the credit to a new Ohio home.

State law adds a disclosure step at the deed stage. Under ORC 319.202, the buyer's value statement must confirm that the seller was asked whether the property gets a tax reduction under section 323.152(A) and whether it was in current agricultural use valuation. If it was, the paperwork has to account for the lost reduction or the recoupment charge before the auditor endorses the deed.

How do I handle unpaid Delaware County tax ahead of a sale?

Get the exact balance from the treasurer before settling on an asking price, and have the closing agent order a payoff figure so the tax is settled out of the sale. The treasurer's website carries a Tax Lien Sales page with a tax lien certificate sale policy, and the auditor's site has a Forfeited Land Sales page, so a long delinquency can end in a county process.

The treasurer's forms page lists a Penalty Remission form. Call (740) 833-2480 to ask whether it applies to a given parcel. Owners who are behind and short on time can also line up a buyer first and let the closing statement show the tax balance as a line item.

Where is the Delaware County auditor's office?

It is at 145 N. Union St., 1st floor, Delaware, OH 43015, and the phone is (740) 833-2900. Hours are Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

Who do I call about a Delaware County tax bill?

Call the Delaware County Treasurer at (740) 833-2480. The treasurer shares the 145 N. Union St. building with the auditor and takes questions on payments, escrow and penalties.

Who can file a Delaware County value complaint?

The owner of taxable real property in the county, the owner's spouse, and a retained professional such as a licensed appraiser, broker or public accountant can file, under ORC 5715.19. The form is on the auditor's forms page, and the Board of Revision handles value only, not the rate.

Did every Delaware County owner get the Inflation Cap Credit?

No. The treasurer's notice says residential and agricultural parcels received it except those in the Dublin, Westerville and Olentangy school districts, and not every property qualifies.

What is the Delaware County property tax rate?

It depends on the parcel's school district, township or city, and voted levies. The auditor posts a Rates of Taxation page and an Effective Tax Rates page, and the parcel's own record shows its figures.

Fairfield County by the numbers

Which Fairfield County offices deal with property tax?

Fairfield County splits property tax among an auditor who values the land, a treasurer who bills and collects, and a Board of Revision that hears value complaints. Most of it happens in Lancaster, the county seat, in or near the building at 210 East Main Street.

The office assesses real property and administers levies and rates.

What kind of county is Fairfield County for a seller?

Fairfield County lies southeast of Columbus and is part of the Columbus metropolitan area. The 2020 census counted 158,921 people, and the 2025 estimate of 169,752 marks a 6.8% rise. Land area is 504 square miles, and QuickFacts shows 65,608 housing units, a typical owner-occupied home value of $298,800 and a median household income of $90,966 for 2020 to 2024.

Cities named on the county's Wikipedia page are Lancaster, Pickerington, Canal Winchester and Reynoldsburg, with Columbus reaching in from the west. The north is flat, glaciated farmland, and the land rises toward foothills along US 33 near Carroll. Buckeye Lake sits partly in the northeast, and the Hocking Hills region lies just across the southern line. School districts include Lancaster City, Pickerington, Reynoldsburg, Canal Winchester, Fairfield Union, Amanda-Clearcreek, Berne Union, Bloom-Carroll, Liberty Union-Thurston, Northern Local, Walnut Township, Southwest Licking and Teays Valley.

How does Fairfield County work out a tax bill?

The treasurer's FAQ gives the recipe: market value times 35% gives assessed value, and assessed value times the effective tax rate for the parcel's taxing district gives the gross tax. The effective rate depends on which school district, township or city the parcel lies in, so two houses of equal value can pay different amounts.

Bills run a year behind. A levy voters pass in a given year applies to that tax year, but the bill is payable the following year. The previous owner's name can stay on a bill for a year after a purchase, because the record shows who owned the parcel on January 1 of the tax year. The FAQ adds that this does not excuse the new owner from paying.

When are Fairfield County property taxes due, and how can I pay?

Payments are due in two installments, and for 2026 the treasurer's page lists February 19 for the first half and July 30 for the second. Both dates have passed. A payment counts on time if it carries a valid US Postal Service postmark on the due date, and private postage meter marks and postdated checks are refused.

  • Mail the check in the envelope that comes with the bill, made out to the Fairfield County Treasurer.
  • Pay in person at 210 East Main Street, Room 105, or use the drive-thru and drop box at 135 W. Chestnut Street, which opens only for the three weeks before a due date.
  • Pay through MuniciPay online, where the e-check fee is $1.00 and cards cost 2.35%, or call the automated line at 740-279-3552.
  • Use the escrow plan to prepay in monthly installments; first-half escrow payments are based on the prior year's tax, and any difference is settled with the February payment.

If no bill arrives, the burden is on the owner. Bills go out in January and June, and not receiving one does not waive a penalty, so call 740-652-7140 if yours has not come by the end of January or the middle of June.

What happens if I fall behind on Fairfield County property tax?

The penalty is 10% of the current tax under ORC 323.17, cut to 5% if the payment lands within the first ten days after the due date. Interest is added to prior delinquencies on August 1 and to unpaid current tax on December 1, according to the treasurer.

A parcel that is more than a year delinquent can be filed with the county prosecutor for sale at a sheriff's auction. Owners whose house is their primary residence can ask for a delinquent tax contract to pay in installments, provided they have not defaulted on an earlier plan; the number for that is 740-652-7149. A penalty remission form exists too, and the FAQ says penalties can be forgiven only in limited circumstances set by law. The treasurer also publishes a delinquent parcel list and a notice about excess funds from tax foreclosure sales.

How do I dispute my value with the Fairfield County Board of Revision?

Download the complaint form from the auditor's Board of Revision page or call 740-652-7030 to have one sent. The treasurer's FAQ says complaints run from December, after the first-half bill is mailed, until March 31, and ORC 5715.19 sets the cutoff at March 31 or the close of first-half collection, whichever is later.

The board sends a hearing date after it receives the form. The FAQ says an attorney is usually unnecessary and the hearing takes under an hour, with anything you submit used to reconsider the appraised value. Having a sale price, an appraisal or repair estimates ready is the practical way to prepare.

What can I look up about my Fairfield County property before selling?

Three online tools cover most of what a seller needs. The auditor's Real Estate Property Search, a new version of which the county announced in June 2026, shows each parcel's value and its Tax tab with the amount due, a Pay This Amount button and prior-year payments in parentheses. The treasurer's site carries the property tax search, the tax FAQ and the delinquent parcel list.

The recorder's land records search holds indexes back to 1800 and documents online from January 1980. The recorder also offers free property fraud and notary fraud alerts, which matter for anyone who owns a vacant or inherited house. Staff will not search records or help prepare a document, and the office does not supply recording forms, so a title company or attorney handles the paperwork. The recorder's number is 740-652-7100.

  • Auditor: parcel number, current value, credits shown on the Tax tab.
  • Treasurer: balance due, escrow account, payment history for escrow customers by phone.
  • Recorder: deed copies, recorded mortgages and releases, fraud alert sign-up.

Which Fairfield County tax credits could change a sale?

Fairfield County has forms for three reductions: homestead for elderly or disabled owners, a farmland valuation for land being farmed, and the owner-occupancy credit. The auditor handles the applications, and the office number is 740-652-7020. In August 2026 the auditor also warned residents about online videos pushing a supposed federal Senior Homeowner Tax Review Request, and said no such federal form exists.

When a deed is filed, ORC 319.202 makes the buyer's value statement report whether the seller says the property carries a reduction and whether it was in agricultural use. If farm valuation applies, a recoupment charge may follow, so a seller with acreage should raise it with the closing agent before accepting a contract.

More questions about Fairfield County, OH Property Tax Guide

Where do I pay Fairfield County property taxes in person?

Go to the Treasurer's Office at 210 East Main Street, Room 105, Lancaster, OH 43130, any weekday between 8 and 4. The drive-thru at 135 W. Chestnut Street operates only in the three weeks before a due date.

What are the 2026 Fairfield County tax due dates?

The treasurer lists February 19, 2026 for the first half and July 30, 2026 for the second half. Both have passed, so ask the treasurer at 740-652-7140 for the schedule that applies to current bills.

What fee does Fairfield County charge to pay online?

The county's payment page lists a $1.00 fee for an e-check and 2.35% for a card through MuniciPay. Mailing a check or paying at the counter avoids the online processing fee.

Does the previous owner's name on my Fairfield County bill matter?

It does not change who owes. The bill keeps the January 1 owner's name until the following year, and the treasurer says the new owner is still responsible for payment.

Can I pay Fairfield County delinquent taxes in installments?

Yes, if the property is your primary residence and you have not defaulted on a prior plan. Call 740-652-7149 or send in the Delinquent Payment Plan Request Form.

Owners can pay the annual bill in one installment early in the year, in two installments, or in monthly installments. The Treasurer posts the 2026 collection dates as follows.

PaymentDate posted by the Treasurer
First half, 2026 collectionFebruary 28, 2026 on the Collection Dates page; March 2, 2026 on the Real Estate Taxes page
Second half, 2026 collectionJuly 20, 2026
Penalty and interestApply to taxes paid after the due date; a missing bill does not avoid them

Source: Franklin County Treasurer. The first-half date moved in 2026, so read the date printed on your own bill instead of an older calendar. Both 2026 dates have passed. Ohio puts the duty on the parcel owner to get a bill in time to pay, and the Treasurer will send a duplicate by phone or online request at 614-525-3438.

Property taxes are billed in arrears and can be paid only after the Auditor assesses them. The Budget Payment Program lets you prepay monthly into an escrow account in your name, which is applied automatically when the semi-annual bill comes due. Under Ohio Revised Code 7.16, the county posts its full tax rate listing on the Columbus Dispatch website.

Mailed payments go to the Franklin County Treasurer with the parcel number and a daytime phone number written on the check, along with the billing statement. Enclose a stamped return envelope addressed to yourself if you want a receipt. The office has a kiosk for credit card payments through its secure payment site. When a payment is returned, the Treasurer reverses it after the bank notifies the office, which normally takes two to three business days, and charges no returned item fee, although a penalty can still apply if the due date is missed.

How does Franklin County value my house?

Ohio law requires a reappraisal of all real property every six years, with an update at the three-year midpoint. Franklin County completed its countywide reappraisal in 2023 and a triennial update in 2026.

Between those cycles the Treasurer says a value changes only for three reasons:

  • physical changes such as a new porch, patio or deck
  • demolition of a structure
  • a Board of Revision decision on a filed complaint

A bill equals the tax rate times the value of the property, so a lower value flows straight to the bill. On the Treasurer's property search, the Distribution tab shows how your bill splits among the school district, municipality, library and other entities.

Where can I contest a Franklin County property value?

Complaints about value start with the Board of Revision. For tax year 2026, the Treasurer's FAQ says the Auditor's office accepts valuation complaints from November 20, 2026 until March 31, 2027, and the Board of Revision page confirms the March 31, 2027 end. The tax year 2025 window has already closed.

The Board of Revision reviews the Auditor's appraised value and can change it based on evidence. Useful documents include a closing statement, a purchase contract or an appraisal. Hearings are held by Zoom, and an in-person hearing can be requested at least 10 days ahead. Some cases go to mediation, which is less formal. The Board hears complaints about value, so the tax dollars you pay and the rate are outside its authority.

A party unhappy with the ruling has 30 days from the date it was mailed to file a notice of appeal with the Ohio Board of Tax Appeals or with the Court of Common Pleas. The notice must also go to the Board of Revision, and to the County Auditor for a court filing.

What tax relief does Franklin County offer?

The Auditor and Treasurer list several programs, each with its own application:

  • Homestead exemption: for owners who turn 65 by the end of the application year, or totally and permanently disabled as of January 1, living in the home as a primary residence. The Auditor's page cites a total income limit of $41,000 for applications tied to a 2025 return. Applications go to Franklin County Auditor, Homestead, 373 S High St, 21st Floor, or to homestead@franklincountyohio.gov.
  • Enhanced homestead exemption: for veterans who are 100% disabled from service-connected injuries and for surviving spouses of public service officers killed in the line of duty. No income test applies, and approval reduces taxes on $50,000 of appraised value.
  • Current Agricultural Use Valuation (CAUV): farmland valued by soil type. Applications and renewals are due the first Monday of March.
  • Penalty remission: file form 23-A with the Treasurer's Office to ask that a late-payment penalty be forgiven.
  • Delinquent tax payment plans: the Treasurer offers plans to bring a past due account current.

Around 40,000 Franklin County parcels receive some tax incentive such as an abatement or a tax increment financing arrangement.

How does a sale change my Franklin County tax situation?

Ownership changes pass through the Auditor ahead of the Recorder, and the county's conveyance fee is $3 per $1,000 of the sale price unless the seller is receiving the homestead exemption, in which case it is $1 per $1,000. Franklin County's transfer charge is $0.50 on every non-exempt transfer.

Ohio law requires the buyer's statement of value to say whether the seller reported a homestead or owner-occupancy reduction on the home and whether the land was in farm use valuation (R.C. 319.202). When a reduction exists, buyer and seller account for the estimated amount between them. A farm use property that leaves the program can face a recoupment charge.

Because bills arrive in arrears, the closing statement is where a seller and buyer divide the year. Ask the title agent for the current payment status from the Treasurer's property search, and ask the Treasurer about any penalty remission before closing. A seller behind on payments can ask the Treasurer about a delinquent payment plan.

What should I know about Franklin County?

Franklin County was established April 30, 1803 and covers about 544 square miles. Columbus is the county seat. The 2020 census counted 1,323,807 people, the most of any Ohio county, and 540,369 households. The county is the center of the Columbus metropolitan area and borders Delaware, Fairfield, Licking, Madison, Pickaway and Union counties.

Property in a city such as Dublin, Gahanna, Hilliard or Westerville is billed by the same county Treasurer, but the tax rate depends on the taxing districts that cover the parcel, such as the school district and municipality.

When is the second half of Franklin County property tax due?

The Treasurer posted July 20, 2026 for the second half of the 2026 collection. Taxes paid after that date accrue penalty and interest, even if a bill never arrived.

Where do I file a Franklin County property value complaint?

With the Board of Revision through the Auditor's office. Tax year 2026 complaints are accepted from November 20, 2026 through March 31, 2027.

Which Franklin County office answers questions about a tax bill?

The Treasurer at 614-525-3438. Value questions go to the Auditor at 614-525-4663, and complaints go to the Board of Revision at 614-525-3913.

Can I pay Franklin County property taxes monthly?

Yes. The Treasurer allows monthly installments and runs a Budget Payment Program that holds prepayments in an escrow account in your name and applies them to the bill.

Is the Franklin County conveyance fee lower for homestead sellers?

Yes. The Auditor's calculator lowers the conveyance fee from $3 to $1 per $1,000 of the sale price when the seller receives the homestead exemption at the time of transfer.

Geauga County by the numbers

Who sets and collects property tax in Geauga County?

Three county offices in Chardon share the work. In Chardon the Auditor puts a value on every parcel, the Treasurer mails the bills and receives the money, and the Board of Revision rules on disputes over value.

Sitting on the Board of Revision are the Auditor, its permanent secretary, the president of the County Commissioners and the Treasurer. The Auditor's office is at 231 Main Street, Suite 1-A, Chardon, Ohio 44024, with a real estate direct line of (440) 279-1617 and a main line of (440) 279-1600.

The Auditor's Tax Info page carries two tools worth bookmarking: a Calculate Your Taxes page that estimates the bill on an existing or hypothetical parcel from the posted tax rates table, and a Tax Rates page. Those rates are approved by the Geauga County Budget Commission, certified by each taxing district to the Auditor, and then adjusted by the state's effective-rate factors each December. The same page lists levy changes for each of the 33 districts, and notes that some levies are non-qualifying, meaning the 10 percent and Owner Occupancy credits do not apply to them.

When are Geauga County property taxes billed and due?

Bills for the first half are issued in January and for the second half in June. The Auditor's property search page says the payment deadlines fall on the second Wednesday in February and the second Wednesday in July.

The Treasurer sends tax bills only by regular mail, and the Auditor's portal warns that any text message asking for a tax payment is fraudulent. The portal also carries a yearly tax calendar for the exact dates.

  • The Treasurer, rather than the Auditor, issues the bills.
  • Any text asking you to pay is a scam, so delete it.
  • Before a closing, request a payoff on the exact parcel from the Treasurer.

How many parcels does the Geauga County Auditor value?

On January 1, 2026 the Auditor's portal counted 52,207 parcels in Geauga County. The Auditor's real estate page says the office must see that every parcel and the buildings on it are fairly and uniformly appraised.

Geauga's 33 taxing districts each carry their own levies, which is why identical houses in different townships or school districts can get different bills.

How often are Geauga County values updated?

State law has every parcel reappraised at six-year intervals, with a mid-cycle update in year three. The Auditor's appraisal office carries out the sexennial reappraisals, the triennial updates and annual new construction valuations, and its field appraisers visit every property that was issued a building or zoning permit during the year.

The Auditor's portal has posted tentative values for tax year 2026, payable in 2027, for owners to search by parcel. The appraisal page lists what changes a value: added square footage, additions, new outbuildings and major improvements that needed a permit. New carpet, appliances, fixtures, landscaping and a new driveway surface do not.

What is the process to dispute my Geauga County valuation?

Begin by asking one of the Auditor's appraisers for an informal review. If you still disagree, a formal complaint goes to the Board of Revision, and the appraisal office wants solid evidence for at least one of these three grounds.

  • The record describes the property wrongly, for instance a carport listed as a garage.
  • The estimate runs above what comparable homes sold for, or above a bank appraisal.
  • Your value is out of line with the estimates on similar homes nearby.

R.C. 5715.19 gives owners until the end of March after the tax year, or until first-half collection closes if that falls later. The Board then has 180 days from the final filing date to rule. While a complaint is open the Treasurer will take payment at your claimed value, and interest accrues on any gap if you lose. A parcel already challenged during the same interim period cannot be challenged again unless it sold at arm's length, lost value to casualty or gained a major improvement.

What tax relief does Geauga County offer homeowners?

The Homestead Exemption shields $29,000 of a home's market value from local taxes, and the Auditor's page puts the average Geauga savings at about $518 a year. The Auditor's own example is that a $100,000 home would be billed as if it were worth $71,000.

  • Seniors: turn 65 by the end of 2026 and keep household income below $41,000, measured as 2025 Ohio adjusted gross income.
  • Disabled owners: certified permanently and totally disabled on January 1, 2026, under the same income cap.
  • Veterans: hold a total (100 percent) service-connected rating and file form DTE 105I.
  • Surviving spouses: of someone who was getting the old exemption, if at least 59 when the spouse died.

File a paper application, DTE 105A, with the Auditor by December 31. The signature must be original, and the office does not accept electronic filing. If the Auditor denies you, form DTE 106B carries the appeal to the Board of Revision. The Auditor also runs an Owner Occupancy Credit tool, the farm CAUV and forestry programs and a destroyed property deduction.

What if a Geauga County house is damaged or destroyed?

The Auditor can lower the value of real estate hurt by fire, flood, ice or other causes, but cannot issue refunds for earlier years. File the damaged property application as soon as possible. The deduction depends on the calendar quarter of the damage.

Damage from January through March earns a 100 percent deduction and April through June earns 75 percent, and the deadline for both is December 31. July through September earns 50 percent with the same deadline. October through December earns 25 percent, with a January 31 deadline. The reduction stays until the property is restored.

How do taxes play out at a Geauga County closing?

Geauga County deeds go to the Auditor for transfer before they are recorded. At the Auditor the fees are $4.00 per $1,000 of transfer value plus $0.50 per parcel, and the tax records are updated as the parcel changes hands.

Get the balance on the parcel from the Treasurer, then confirm with your title company who pays the February and July installments. The Auditor's real estate page also links a Forfeited Land Sale page, which is the place to look if taxes on a parcel were missed.

What do Geauga County's housing statistics show?

The 2020 Census counted 95,397 people in Geauga County. Owners occupy 87.2 percent of the housing stock, the median home they own is worth $331,100, and the median household earns $107,860. The county issued 180 building permits in 2025.

Geauga dates to 1806 and spans about 400 square miles of land. Its municipalities include Chardon, Burton, Middlefield and South Russell, and a November 2024 vote dissolved the Village of Aquilla.

When are Geauga County property taxes due?

The second Wednesday in February covers the first half and the second Wednesday in July covers the second half. The Treasurer mails the bills ahead of each date, in January and June.

How much can the Geauga County homestead exemption save?

The exemption shields $29,000 of market value, and the Auditor estimates average savings of about $518 a year. You must apply on paper with the Auditor by December 31 and meet the age or disability and income rules.

Where does a Geauga County value dispute start?

Ask the Auditor's appraisal office for an informal review first. If that fails, a complaint to the Board of Revision must reach the Auditor by the end of the following March, or when first-half collection closes if that is later.

Will the Geauga County Treasurer text me a tax bill?

No. The Treasurer sends bills only by regular mail. A text message asking for a tax payment is fraudulent and should be deleted.

Which number reaches the Geauga County real estate tax staff?

Questions about values, exemptions and credits go to the Auditor's real estate line, (440) 279-1617. The main Auditor number is (440) 279-1600, answered on weekdays between 8:00 and 4:30.

Which office appraises a Greene County parcel?

Appraisal falls to the Greene County Auditor, who values land and buildings at estimated market value. Ohio taxes 35 percent of that figure, as the county's appraisal page explains.

The county's sexennial revaluation wraps up before 2027 begins, and bills sent during 2027 carry the new numbers. A mid-cycle update arrives every three years. Its real estate department maintains files on over 73,000 parcels, and the phone line is (937) 562-5072.

  • Current Agricultural Use Value (CAUV) and certified forest land reductions
  • Homestead credit, owner-occupied credit and non-business credit

  • Property transfers and conveyances

What do Census figures say about Greene County housing?

Xenia holds the courthouse, while Beavercreek has the most residents. Greene spreads over roughly 414 square miles of southwestern Ohio land within the Dayton metro area, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate of 174,322 people runs 3.8 percent over its 2020 base.

Survey years 2020 through 2024 show a $252,200 median for homes their owners live in, a $87,309 median household income, and 68.0 percent of dwellings held by their occupants. Districts that levy school tax here include Beavercreek, Bellbrook-Sugarcreek, Cedar Cliff, Fairborn, Greeneview, Xenia Community and Yellow Springs, plus the Greene County Career Center.

What are Greene County's tax deadlines and late penalties?

State law defaults to December 31 and June 20 for the two halves, and extensions are possible. The treasurer calls a payment late starting the day after the date shown on your bill, with no extensions for individuals.

Under R.C. 323.121, an unpaid half picks up a 10 percent charge. Pay the whole amount inside ten days and the treasurer waives half of that charge. Interest accrues afterward on delinquent balances.

Active-duty military owners can apply to the Military Assistance Program for more time. A penalized owner may file form DTE 23A, a remission request listed on the county forms page.

A treasurer notice on mailed checks explains that, since late December 2025, a postmark generally shows when sorting equipment first touched the envelope, possibly days after you dropped it off. Send early, ask a clerk for a postmark stamped by hand, or choose another way to pay.

What payment options does the Greene County Treasurer offer?

Walk-in payments and mail both go to 15 Greene St., Xenia, OH 45385. Mail needs a USPS postmark, because a private meter will not count. Checks can also go into a locked curbside box out front, available at any hour while collection is open.

  • Point & Pay online, where the vendor charges 2.35 percent (minimum $2.00) on credit cards, a flat $2.95 on debit cards and $0.75 on eChecks.

  • Semi-annual electronic withdrawal during normal collection periods.

Ohio law (R.C. 323.13) wants any change of tax-bill address in writing to the treasurer, so a seller who moves should send a signed form.

What is the process for disputing a Greene County value?

The vehicle is form DTE 1, a Complaint Against the Valuation of Real Property, turned in at the auditor. March 31 of the following tax year is the date on the auditor's page, and R.C. 5715.19 adds the close of first-half collection if that falls later. A Board of Revision hears the case and looks at value only.

County guidance for filers lists the evidence that carries weight:

  • Proof tied to your own parcel, since broad talk about the market says little about it.
  • For rental or commercial property, income and expense records going back up to three years.
  • For an appraisal, an appraiser who agrees to testify before the board.
  • For a sale, the realtor's listing history with list price and days on market.
  • For condition problems, photos, finished work and written repair estimates.

A ruling can be taken further, to the Ohio Board of Tax Appeals or the common pleas court. A notice of appeal has to be filed inside 30 days of the decision's mailing date.

What tax breaks can Greene County homeowners claim?

R.C. 323.152 gives a homestead reduction to resident owners aged 65 and up, owners with a permanent and total disability, and some surviving spouses aged 59 to 64. The text names a $25,000 true-value figure and a $30,000 income limit, both indexed yearly, plus $50,000 for disabled veterans and for spouses of public service officers who died on duty. The auditor can give the adjusted amounts for the tax year.

Matching applications on the county forms page include DTE 105A (seniors and disabled owners), DTE 105B (continuing), DTE 105C (owner occupancy) and DTE 105I (disabled veterans). Farmland owners use DTE 109 for CAUV, and DTE 26 covers property that was damaged or destroyed. Manufactured home owners have a separate set that includes DTE 50.

What follows a missed Greene County tax payment?

A county lien for taxes ranks first and best against the real property. Once the auditor hands over the Delinquent Land Tax Duplicate, the prosecutor can file foreclosure on the treasurer's behalf. To pay off a parcel that is already in foreclosure, call the delinquent tax division at (937) 562-5672.

A seller with a balance can ask the closing agent to pay it from the proceeds, so request a payoff figure early.

What does the auditor require when a Greene County house changes hands?

The recorder gets the deed only after the auditor has transferred it. Expect to supply DTE 100 (or DTE 100 EX if exempt), map department approval, a grantor name identical to the prior deed, and a notarized signature. Per the auditor's page, the conveyance fee is $2.00 per thousand dollars of price, with $0.50 charged per parcel, and an online calculator is available.

R.C. 319.202 puts those charges on the grantor, and the buyer's statement has to address homestead reductions and CAUV status that might lead to a recoupment charge. Have the closing agent show how each installment bill is divided.

Where is the Greene County treasurer's counter?

At 15 Greene St. in Xenia. A curbside box out front takes checks around the clock while collection is open, and Point & Pay online adds the vendor's fee.

When must a Greene County valuation complaint be filed?

By March 31 of the following tax year, or the close of first-half collection when that is later. Submit form DTE 1 to the county auditor with evidence about your own parcel.

Does Greene County offer a monthly way to pay tax?

Yes. The treasurer's monthly budget plan runs by mail or electronic withdrawal, and (937) 562-5289 is the number to enroll. A semi-annual withdrawal option also exists.

Who owes the conveyance fee on a Greene County sale?

The seller, as grantor, pays the auditor before the deed reaches the recorder. The county page states $2.00 per thousand dollars of price, and $0.50 per parcel.

Cities include Blue Ash, Norwood, Wyoming, Springdale and Sharonville, and townships run from Colerain and Green to Anderson and Sycamore.

What payment dates does the Hamilton County Treasurer use?

A December 2025 announcement from the treasurer set February 10 and July 10 as the permanent due dates, with bills mailed roughly three weeks earlier. In 2026 the first half fell due on February 10, while the second half slid to July 24 with bills mailed July 2. Some county pages still speak of January and June, so trust the date on your bill.

Per the treasurer's FAQ, a payment that is up to ten days late draws 5 percent, and after that state law raises the charge to 10 percent. Penalized taxpayers can ask for a waiver. A mailed check is timely with a postmark on the due date or earlier, yet the Postal Service stamps the date its sorting machines first handle an envelope. Near a deadline, the treasurer recommends having the post office stamp it by hand.

Where and how do you pay the Hamilton County Treasurer?

The office sits at 138 E. Court St., Room 402, Cincinnati, OH 45202, and takes visitors weekdays between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. outside holidays. Call (513) 946-4800. Only the counter accepts cash; checks are made out to the Hamilton County Treasurer, with the stub or the parcel number on the memo line.

  • Point & Pay, online or at 1-877-764-3524, where the vendor (not the county) keeps a $1.00 eCheck fee or 2.35 percent on cards.
  • Mail to the Room 402 address, postmarked no later than the due date.
  • Hand delivery, including a drop box just inside the main entrance of the county building during business hours.
  • Installment prepayment, arranged through 946-4788.

An owner who splits one parcel's payment across methods should email payments.treasurer@hamiltoncountyohio.gov so each piece posts correctly. Once a bill is paid, no duplicate can be printed, so ask for copies before the deadline.

What is the Inflation Cap Credit in Hamilton County?

House Bill 186 limits inflation-driven growth from unvoted levies that would flow to schools sitting at the 20-mill floor, with a 2-mill floor for career-technical districts. The first credit reflected inflation across tax years 2023 to 2025 and landed on 2026 second-half bills. About 80 percent of the county's parcels lie in an affected district, and a parcel in both a school and a career district gets both credits added up.

Butler County JVSD appears on the same page at $11.64 (Class 1) and $0.10 (Class 2). Critics cited there say the credit cuts money reaching schools.

How does a Hamilton County owner contest a valuation?

The Board of Revision accepts owner complaints from January 1 through March 31 each year on form DTE 1 (DTE 1M for manufactured homes). Postmark by March 31, skip email, and remember that a filing begins a legal proceeding. Three officials sit on the board, the county auditor, the treasurer and the commission president, and they may send designees.

Taxes are off the table; the board rules on value, and the owner carries the burden of proof. Its examples of useful evidence:

  • For a recent arm's-length purchase: closing statement, purchase contract or the sale appraisal.
  • For a value dispute: sales of similar homes by size, type and age, or an appraisal effective January 1 of the tax year.
  • For serious condition problems: certified repair estimates and dated photos.
  • For rental property: income and expense statements.

Evidence goes in with the complaint or up to ten days ahead of the hearing. A hearing lasts around 15 minutes, and a certified-mail result follows in six to eight weeks. Challenging that result means filing with the Ohio Board of Tax Appeals or the Court of Common Pleas, 30 days counting from the mailing.

What does Hamilton County do about delinquent property tax?

A delinquent contract lets an owner pay back taxes on a schedule while keeping current ones paid. While the contract stays in good standing, the parcel is shielded from added penalties, interest, tax foreclosure and a lien sale. The line to start one is (513) 946-4800.

Balances left after the June collection are certified delinquent in November and can be sold as a lien the next October. The sale tends to fall near the second week of October, and the county bundles liens for financial institutions rather than individual investors. A sold lien adds fees, and the holder may begin foreclosure if nothing is repaid within a year. Tax foreclosure is a lawsuit the county prosecutor files for the treasurer, with a typical 28 days for the owner to answer and sheriff sales held online.

What should a Hamilton County seller check on taxes at closing?

Each parcel gets its own bill, so a home on several parcels needs every bill totaled before the payoff. The stadium tax credit is automatic when a property already receives the 2.5 percent rollback.

While a Board of Revision complaint is pending, R.C. 5715.19 lets the owner tender tax figured on the claimed value, which the treasurer may accept. Request a payoff covering both halves before the closing date, and ask whether a delinquent contract is active.

More questions about Hamilton County, OH Property Tax Guide

Which dates does Hamilton County use for property tax?

February 10 and July 10 under the permanent schedule, though the 2026 second half moved to July 24. The date printed on the bill controls.

By when can I dispute my Hamilton County value?

March 31, after a window that opens January 1. A postmark by that date is required, email is refused, and evidence should accompany the complaint.

How much extra does a late Hamilton County payment cost?

Five percent in the first ten days, then 10 percent, according to the treasurer's FAQ. Penalized owners can apply for a waiver.

Does Hamilton County accept cash for property tax?

Yes, at the counter only: 138 E. Court St., Room 402. Mailed payments must be a personal check, cashier's check or money order.

If my Hamilton County value rises, do taxes rise by the same share?

No. The auditor says levies, credits and exemptions drive the bill, so a 20 percent value gain does not mean 20 percent more tax.

Who runs property tax in Highland County, Ohio?

Three Hillsboro offices split the work. The auditor sets values and keeps the tax list, the treasurer sends bills and takes payment, and the recorder files the deeds that change the name on a parcel. The auditor's own description calls that office the county's chief fiscal officer and its appraiser-in-chief for real estate, and says it also hands collected tax out to villages, townships and school districts.

Highland County offices that touch a property tax bill, with contact details from the county's pages

The auditor's website pairs a parcel search with a GIS map, sales reports and a tax estimator.

How is a Highland County house valued for tax?

According to the auditor's FAQ, values are revisited every three years, and Ohio taxes 35% of appraised market value. Millage for the school district, township or village and any levies at the parcel's location then turns that taxable value into a bill.

The county lists five public school districts: Bright Local, Fairfield Local, Greenfield Exempted, Hillsboro City and Lynchburg-Clay Local. Two neighbors on one road can be billed at different rates if a district line runs between them, so pull the parcel's own record instead of copying a nearby bill.

The auditor counts 32,381 parcels as of 2024. The Census Bureau counts 19,196 housing units, so parcels outnumber homes by a wide margin. The gap points to farmland, woodland and vacant lots, and it makes the farm valuation rules further down worth reading even for a town seller.

What were the 2026 payment dates in Highland County?

The treasurer's page printed March 13, 2026 for the first half and August 7, 2026 for the second. Both dates have passed, so a seller who closed after either date should ask the treasurer to confirm each half was posted. Future dates differ, and the same page is where they appear.

Payment options on that page include an online link and a toll-free line, 1-844-920-3600. By mail, the address is P.O. Box 824, Hillsboro, OH 45133. The treasurer's own phone is 937-393-9951.

Back taxes belong to the same office. The auditor's tools menu includes a delinquency report, and the treasurer can say what a past-due balance would add to a payoff. A title company will request that payoff whatever the answer.

Where do you contest a Highland County valuation?

An owner who thinks the value is wrong files a complaint with the auditor, and the county Board of Revision hears it. Section 5715.19 sets the deadline at March 31 of the next tax year, or the day first-half collection closes if that is later. The complaint has to state how much overvaluation or undervaluation it claims.

Three forms on the auditor's site cover most cases:

  • DTE 1 for a complaint about the value of real property.
  • DTE 1M for a manufactured or mobile home taxed like real property.
  • DTE 2 for a complaint about an assessment other than market value.

While a complaint is pending the owner may pay on the value claimed, and the statute makes the complainant hand over all evidence in the owner's knowledge. A recent arm's-length sale is the strongest proof, and the auditor's sales report shows what neighbors' parcels brought.

Which Highland County forms reduce a tax bill?

The auditor sorts relief forms by type. The county's page lists:

  • Homestead: DTE 105A for seniors, disabled persons and surviving spouses, DTE 105I for disabled veterans and their surviving spouses, and DTE 105K for surviving spouses of public service officers killed in the line of duty.
  • Owner occupancy: DTE 105C for real property and DTE 56 for taxed manufactured homes.
  • Damage: DTE 26 for destroyed or damaged real property and DTE 49 for a manufactured home.
  • Exemptions: DTE 23 for tax-exempt owners and DTE 23V for veterans' and fraternal organizations.

Filing windows and income limits move with the tax year, so ask the Highland County Auditor which apply to you before relying on a form from memory.

How does the farm valuation program work in Highland County?

The current agricultural use valuation program taxes qualifying farmland on its farm income instead of its market price. Land of 10 or more acres, not counting the homesite, qualifies if used exclusively for agriculture. Smaller tracts qualify with gross income of at least $2,500 in each of the past three years. The first application costs $25 and must be filed before the first Monday in March, and renewals are mailed to owners each year.

Leaving the program is expensive. The county's FAQ says land removed from it owes a recoupment charge equal to three years of the tax savings, whether the owner missed a renewal or changed the use. Woodland cannot take both the farm program and the older forestry savings, and the farm program needs a management plan from a licensed forester that the auditor approves.

A sale brings the program into the paperwork. Section 319.202 has the buyer's statement report whether the parcel was enrolled, and the auditor's forms include DTE 102 for such a conveyance. A farm seller should ask for the likely recoupment figure before accepting an offer.

What tax records should a Highland County seller gather before listing?

A short folder saves days with a buyer's title company. Pull these items from the county's own sites:

  • The parcel record from the auditor's search page, which shows the owner of record, the valuation and the tax history.
  • The treasurer's payment status for both halves of the current year, plus any past-due balance from the delinquency report.
  • Proof of any homestead or owner occupancy reduction you now receive, because the buyer's value statement must say whether the seller's taxes are reduced.
  • Any farm valuation enrollment, with the three-year recoupment exposure in mind.

The auditor's conveyance fee calculator, which includes a parcel transfer fee, gives a rough closing cost before the county's final figure. The auditor's page lists the Ohio conveyance statement forms, DTE 100 and DTE 100EX, next to the homestead and farm conveyance statements, so the right paper is easy to find.

What do the numbers say about Highland County sellers?

The county covers about 553 square miles of hilly land with Hillsboro as its seat. The Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 43,823 people. Its 2020 to 2024 survey shows 74.3% of occupied homes owner-occupied, a median value of $168,900, median household income of $65,785 and a poverty rate of 14.6%. The mean commute is 29.1 minutes.

The Census also records 733 employer establishments and a 4.9% rise in employment from 2022 to 2023, with health care and social assistance receipts near $195 million in 2022. A buyer's lender reads the same data, which is one reason an accurate tax estimate belongs in the listing file.

A seller behind on payments can begin at the treasurer, then ask the auditor for the parcel's tax history before negotiating. The recorder and auditor share the 119 Governor Foraker Place address, so a deed question and a valuation question can often be handled in one trip.

More questions about Highland County, OH Property Tax Guide

Who bills property tax in Highland County?

The Highland County Treasurer. The mailing address is P.O. Box 824 in Hillsboro, the phone is 937-393-9951, and the treasurer's page also takes payments online.

What share of market value does Ohio tax?

35%. The Highland County Auditor's FAQ gives that figure and says values are revisited every three years.

What is the deadline for a valuation complaint?

March 31 of the next tax year, or the close of first-half collection if that falls later. File form DTE 1 with the auditor and expect a Board of Revision hearing.

Does the county have a farmland program?

Yes, current agricultural use valuation. It requires exclusive agricultural use and a $25 first application filed before the first Monday in March.

What happens if farmland stops qualifying?

The owner pays a recoupment charge equal to the tax savings of the last three years. Ask the auditor for an estimate before you sign a sale contract.

Lake County by the numbers

Which Lake County offices handle property tax?

Valuing and billing are separate jobs in Painesville. The Auditor sets values for over 111,000 parcels, and the Treasurer mails bills and takes payment. By the Auditor's account, Ohio law wants a full reappraisal on a six year cycle and a value update midway, in year three. That office also says it has no power over the amount of tax, because voter-approved levies drive the rate.

Numbers to keep handy: the Auditor's real estate staff at (440) 350-2532 for owner address changes and credit questions, the Treasurer's billing line at (440) 350-2516 and the delinquent tax division at 440-350-2473. The Treasurer's main office keeps counter hours from 8:00 to 4:30 on weekdays at 105 Main Street, and any parcel can be looked up through the Auditor's real property search.

When are Lake County real estate taxes due?

Ohio bills real estate tax in two halves. The Lake County Treasurer's page lists the dates by the year the tax is payable, and the first set below has already passed.

Lake County real estate tax due dates as listed on the Treasurer's welcome page
Tax year and payable yearFirst halfSecond half
2025 tax, payable 2026Wednesday, February 25, 2026Wednesday, August 5, 2026

Pay after the deadline and a 10 percent penalty is added, with interest running twice a year on balances the county certifies as unpaid. A postal postmark on or before the date counts. The Treasurer quotes section 323.13 for a rule many owners miss: the tax is owed whether or not a bill reached you. Call if nothing shows up by February 1 or July 1. The Auditor's FAQ says mailings go out in mid-January and mid-June, with payment due roughly 20 to 30 days afterward. Manufactured homes run on their own calendar, also posted by the Treasurer.

How do you challenge a Lake County property value?

A Lake County owner can contest the valuation but never the rate. The filing season for a complaint on form DTE 1 runs January 1 to March 31 every year, and the Treasurer's notices show the next one opening January 1, 2027.

  • A three person panel hears the case: the Auditor, the Treasurer and the commissioners' president.
  • Bring proof with the complaint, or file it at least five days before your hearing date.
  • Expect roughly a quarter hour for a house, then a written decision about two to three weeks later.
  • Evidence the county names: a recent arm's length sale, a purchase agreement or listing, an appraisal dated to the January 1 lien date, damage photos, an insurance value, a broker's market analysis, or construction cost for a newer home including land.
  • Arguments the Board says it cannot weigh: how much your bill went up in percent, and how nearby parcels were valued.

Unhappy with the ruling? Form DTE 4 takes the case to the state Board of Tax Appeals within 30 days of the mailing date, and the county Court of Common Pleas is the other route. An appraiser whose report you submit has to show up and testify to it.

What tax relief applies in Lake County after the 2025 reform bills?

The Treasurer's notice says five property tax reform bills, Ohio House Bills 186, 335, 124, 129 and 309, were signed on December 19, 2025, with adjustments phased in over three years. The first affects the July 2026 bill, where applicable credits or reductions are printed. Residential, agricultural and most business properties qualify without an application, and the Treasurer advises contacting your mortgage company once the credit shows so the escrow payment can be adjusted.

The notice also says the homestead credit is doubled for 2026 tax payable in 2027, while the owner occupancy credit is not. For the details, call the Auditor's real estate desk at 440-350-2532. The Auditor's about page describes the homestead exemption as means tested for new participants, so ask for the current household income limit before you apply.

How are Lake County property taxes handled when a house sells?

An ordinary sale settles the current year's tax at closing, usually through a title company. The county's pro-rating page is written for sheriff sales: after a sale is confirmed, the Treasurer gives the total due at that time and prorates the following year's tax from the current year's full-year real estate tax plus long-term assessments such as lighting or storm water. The proration starts 90 days after the sheriff sale, and requests go to the Treasurer by email. The figure is an estimate, and the Treasurer is not responsible for later garbage bills, levy changes or value changes.

The deed transfer charge is a separate line at the Auditor, listed in the FAQ as $4.00 per $1,000 of price plus fifty cents for each parcel. Section 319.202 assigns it to the seller. A seller enrolled in the Treasurer's automatic payment plan should also know that a final bill is never drawn through that plan, so the closing agent has to pay it.

What if Lake County property tax is behind?

The Treasurer's pages lay out what happens as a balance ages:

  • A delinquent payment plan for primary residences and manufactured homes runs two years, with a down payment equal to half a year's tax and an appointment required.
  • A tax lien sale can include a property with delinquency in three billing cycles after multiple notices and newspaper publication, and the page says it is not a sale of the property. An administrative fee of $100.00 applies with the first notice and $200.00 on the sale date, and the sale is generally held every fall.
  • The payment plan page says lien sales can lead to 18 percent interest and added fees.
  • The Treasurer holds the first and best lien on real property. A lien purchaser can ask for foreclosure if the lien is not repaid or on a plan within 18 months, and the county prosecutor can also file in the Treasurer's name, which may lead to a sheriff sale.

A seller who owes back tax can still sell if the payoff clears at closing, so ask the delinquent tax division for a written payoff figure before signing a contract.

What do the numbers say about Lake County?

Lake County has the least land of any Ohio county at 227 square miles, yet its 979 square mile total makes it the third largest, because the lake bed off its 31 mile shoreline counts. The Census Bureau estimate for July 2025 is 232,217 residents in 107,571 housing units. Three of every four households own (75.8 percent), a typical owned home is worth about $214,100 in the 2020 to 2024 survey, and owners with a mortgage report median monthly costs of $1,500.

The Auditor's about page lists the taxing units that share each bill: five townships, nine villages, nine cities, ten school districts and eight library systems. Painesville holds the county offices and Mentor has the biggest population, and a parcel's total rate depends on which of those districts it sits in.

More questions about Lake County, OH Property Tax Guide

When are Lake County real estate taxes due for 2026 tax payable in 2027?

Pay by February 24, 2027 for the first half and July 21, 2027 for the second, per the Treasurer. The 2025 bills closed out on August 5, 2026.

Can I appeal my Lake County property tax bill?

Only the value is open to challenge. The rate comes from levies, and the Auditor says the Board does not hear complaints about taxes. Use form DTE 1 during the January 1 to March 31 season.

What does Lake County charge the seller to transfer the deed?

The Auditor's FAQ lists $4.00 per $1,000 of price and $0.50 per parcel. It splits that into a state piece of $1.00 and a county piece of $3.00, the latter passed by the commissioners on March 26, 1990.

What is the penalty on late Lake County property tax?

Ten percent, with twice-a-year interest on certified balances. A missing bill is no excuse under section 323.13 as the Treasurer cites it. A payment plan can keep the debt from growing.

Can a Lake County homeowner who is behind on tax arrange a payment plan?

Yes, for a primary residence or manufactured home. The plan lasts two years, starts with an appointment and a down payment equal to half a year of tax, and is arranged at 440-350-2473.

Licking County by the numbers

Which part of central Ohio does Licking County cover?

Licking County sits in central Ohio, with Newark as the county seat. Wikipedia says the legislature created it from part of Fairfield County on January 30, 1808, and that it was organized on March 1, 1808. About 683 square miles of it is land, a footprint that ranks third among Ohio counties, and it forms part of the Columbus metropolitan area.

Seven counties touch it: Knox, Coshocton, Muskingum, Perry, Fairfield, Franklin and Delaware. Interstate 70 and U.S. 40 are the named through routes. Its municipalities include six cities: Heath, Johnstown, New Albany, Newark, Pataskala and Reynoldsburg. Manufacturing is a large employer, and Intel, Armstrong World Industries, Invenergy and Atkore are the named manufacturers, and farming still ranks the county 11th among Ohio's 88 counties for products sold.

A farm near Utica, a lot in Newark and a new build in New Albany fall into different school, township and city taxing districts, so equal values do not guarantee equal bills. Wikipedia notes that New Albany alone adds more than 100 homes a year beside a nine-million-square-foot business park, which keeps pressure on land values at the county's western edge.

How pricey and how full is Licking County's housing stock?

The Census Bureau QuickFacts page for Licking County puts the population at 185,564 for July 2025, against 178,501 in April 2020, a gain of 4.0 percent. The housing profile from the 2020 to 2024 survey period:

  • Owner-occupied homes carry a median value of $275,200.
  • Homeownership reaches 73.7 percent among 68,620 households.
  • Carrying costs average $1,693 a month with a loan and $631 free and clear.
  • Tenants pay $1,078 in gross rent at the median.
  • Half of households earn more than $84,426.
  • The July 2025 count of housing units: 73,930.
  • Seniors make up 19.7 percent of residents, and 11,370 are veterans.

Land area measures 682.43 square miles. Wikipedia's summary of the 2020 census adds that two thirds of residents, 66.2 percent, lived in urban areas.

Who runs value and collection for Licking County parcels?

The county splits the job between two desks at 20 South Second Street in Newark. The auditor determines taxable values, certifies rates, administers the reduction programs and acts as secretary to the Board of Revision. The treasurer bills and collects real estate, manufactured home, estate and hotel and motel taxes plus special assessments.

  • Auditor: (740) 670-5040, weekdays from 8:30 AM until 4:30 PM, closed on holidays.
  • Treasurer: 740-670-5010, on the same schedule.
  • Online lookup: both offices point to the county's OnTrac site for parcel search and tax information.
  • Deed work: starting May 1, 2026 the auditor stops same-day processing of conveyances, exempts, splits and merges at 4 p.m.

Money collected by other county departments also lands with the treasurer, who invests county funds under Ohio law.

What did the 2026 triennial update do to Licking County values?

The auditor published a public notice, citing Ohio Revised Code 5713.01, that the 2026 Triennial Update of Licking County property values is complete. Owners can review the new values on OnTrac or at the auditor's counter during weekday office hours. Look up your own parcel on OnTrac to see what changed.

The Ohio Department of Taxation schedule puts Licking in the middle of a six-year cycle: an update in 2026 and the next full reappraisal in 2029. The table shows how neighboring counties line up on that same schedule.

What do Licking County owners owe if an installment is late?

Real estate tax comes in two installments. The exact deadlines print on each bill, and they can shift from one year to the next, so read the bill or phone 740-670-5010.

Section 323.121 sets the consequences. Missing an installment adds ten percent to what is unpaid, though a catch-up inside ten days cuts that charge in half. Interest on old balances starts the month after the second-half deadline and is posted again on December 1.

Mailing works if the Postal Service postmark falls on or before the last day. A postage-meter stamp from a private machine fails that test, under section 323.12.

How does an owner contest a Licking County value?

The auditor receives the complaint and hands it to the Board of Revision. Section 5715.19 sets the filing date at March 31 after the tax year, unless first-half collection closes later. A stamped postmark serves as the date of a mailed complaint.

  • Owners, their spouses and certain licensed professionals working for the owner can sign the filing.
  • A parcel gets one complaint per interim period. Exceptions cover an arm's length sale, damage from a casualty, a major improvement, or a 15 percent swing in occupancy.
  • Hearing notice goes out at least ten days ahead, and the board has 180 days after the filing deadline to rule.
  • During the dispute the treasurer takes a payment based on the owner's claimed value.
  • Put every piece of evidence in front of the board, because material held back can be excluded on appeal.

Ask the auditor's office for the current complaint form and any filing instructions before you prepare the paperwork.

What does a Licking County seller meet at the auditor's counter?

Before the recorder sees a deed, the auditor must. Section 319.202 has the grantee file a value statement and has the auditor mark the deed with the fee collected. The statement also covers any tax reduction or farm-use valuation that could pass to the buyer.

The grantor covers the state conveyance fee at this step. An added county levy exists only if commissioners enacted one under section 322.02, which limits it to 30 cents for every $100. Phone the auditor at (740) 670-5040 to learn whether Licking County has one. Farmland sellers should flag any past farm-use enrollment to the title company, because recoupment rides on the same filing.

Arrive before 4 p.m. if the transfer must clear that day.

How can a Licking County seller check a parcel before listing?

Both the auditor and the treasurer direct visitors to OnTrac, the county's online property site. The treasurer's page labels it the place for tax information and property search, and describes the site as available around the clock, so a seller can check a parcel on a weekend before a closing.

Records of the deed itself live at the recorder's office in the same building, which accepts documents for recording between 8:30 AM and 4:15 PM on weekdays. Buyers' title companies pull the tax record and the recorded history together before setting a closing. A delinquent balance gets settled with the treasurer, whose office collects overdue real estate tax and assessments.

Special assessments sit with the treasurer as well. Ask which ones are open on the parcel so the closing figures include them.

Which number reaches the right Licking County tax office?

Dial the treasurer at 740-670-5010 about payments and the auditor at (740) 670-5040 about values. Both sit at 20 South Second Street in Newark.

When is the next full reappraisal in Licking County?

The Ohio Department of Taxation schedule lists 2029 as the next reappraisal year for Licking County. The 2026 triennial update has already been completed.

Can I contest my Licking County value every year?

No, the statute allows one complaint per parcel in each interim period. A second one needs a qualifying event: an arm's length sale, casualty damage, a substantial improvement, or a 15 percent occupancy change.

Is there a county transfer tax on a Licking County sale?

Ask the auditor, since the tax exists only where commissioners passed a resolution for it. The state conveyance fee is a separate charge that the seller pays at the auditor's counter.

What if I skip a Licking County installment?

Ten percent is added to the unpaid half, and a payment inside ten days earns a 50 percent reduction of that charge. Interest then builds on overdue balances, so call the treasurer early.

Lorain County by the numbers

What makes Lorain County different from its Ohio neighbors?

Lorain County runs along Lake Erie in northeastern Ohio, with Elyria as the seat and the city of Lorain as the largest community. Wikipedia reports 923 square miles in total, of which 432 square miles, or 47 percent, is water, so it ranks as Ohio's fourth-largest county by area while holding only 491 square miles of land. It was physically established in 1822 and became judicially independent in 1824, and it sits inside the Cleveland metropolitan area. Oberlin College is based here.

Cuyahoga, Medina, Ashland, Huron and Erie counties surround it. Nine cities share the territory: Amherst, Avon, Avon Lake, Elyria, Lorain, North Ridgeville, Oberlin, Sheffield Lake and Vermilion. Twenty public school districts have ground in the county, from Elyria and Lorain to Avon, Firelands, Keystone and Oberlin, so a tax bill depends heavily on which district a house falls in. The Ohio Turnpike carries Interstates 80 and 90 through, with Interstate 480, U.S. 6, U.S. 20 and State Route 2 as other major roads.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Lorain County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What does the Census Bureau say about Lorain County housing?

The Census Bureau QuickFacts table for Lorain County estimates 323,219 residents for 2025, compared with 312,980 at the April 2020 base, a 3.3 percent gain. Housing and income measures:

  • A typical owned home is worth $223,200.
  • Owners occupy 74.0 percent of 127,544 households.
  • Ownership costs $1,525 a month with a mortgage and $629 without.
  • Rent runs $966 gross.
  • Household income stands at $73,347.
  • 139,777 housing units existed in July 2025, and builders took out 1,082 permits during 2025.
  • Seniors are 22.3 percent of the population.

The auditor's own site counts about 172,000 parcels as of 2024.

Who sends and who collects the Lorain County tax bill?

Both work out of the Lorain County Administration Building, 226 Middle Avenue, Elyria. The auditor occupies Room 200 and answers at 440-329-5207. The posted schedule is Monday through Thursday with a 4:30 close, and transfers stop at 4:00; a notice adds that the commissioners restored Friday service by funding the office through the end of 2026. The treasurer has Room 201 and (440) 329-5787, with weekday hours that end at 4:30.

Collection belongs to the treasurer, and the auditor points tax questions there. The treasurer also offers an escrow plan for monthly prepayment of current taxes, open to owners with no delinquency.

How did the 2024 reappraisal and House Bill 186 change Lorain County bills?

Lorain County was reappraised in 2024. The auditor's FAQ on House Bill 186, which took effect on March 20, 2026, explains the follow-up: an Inflation Cap Credit applies automatically when school-related taxes rise faster than inflation after a reappraisal. It shows as INFLATION CAP CREDIT in the Summary of Charges, and the credit on 2026 second-half bills corrects increases that came from the 2024 reappraisal. Anyone who paid before the credit posted needs to do nothing, because the overpayment carries into the next first-half bill. The law did not change appraised values.

The auditor also stresses that a rise in value does not equal the same rise in tax, because a levy raises a fixed dollar amount and the millage adjusts as values move.

What were the Lorain County installment dates in 2026?

The treasurer's site listed February 13, 2026 for the first half and July 31, 2026 for the second, flagging the later date as a change tied to the House Bill 186 inflation cap credit. Both have passed. The auditor certified the 2025 real estate rates for payment in 2026 on January 7, 2026.

A late half costs ten percent under Ohio Revised Code 323.121, reduced by half if the money arrives within ten days. Title and mortgage companies that generate and print their own bills skip the duplicate bill fee. For the dates on a later bill, read the bill or call 440-329-5787.

How does a Lorain County owner dispute a value?

A Complaint Against the Valuation of Real Property goes in after January 1 and by March 31. For tax year 2025 the last day was March 31, 2026. Rules on the auditor's page:

  • Signature and notary seal are required, and owner, address and parcel numbers must be right.
  • Ordinary mail works, and the postmark counts as the filing date.
  • Filing costs nothing.
  • The county allows a single complaint in each three-year stretch between reappraisals and updates. A sale at arm's length, a substantial improvement, casualty damage or a 15 percent commercial occupancy shift reopens the door.
  • Complaints may also challenge farm-use determinations or property classification.

Local school boards may also petition the board. The hearing schedule and a case search are on the auditor's site.

Which Lorain County tax reductions matter at a sale?

Three programs come up at Lorain County closings. Ohio's homestead exemption removes the tax on $29,000 of market value for a qualifying home in tax year 2025. The enhanced version, at $58,000, serves disabled veterans and the surviving spouse of a public safety officer killed on duty. Eligible owners are 65 or older, permanently and totally disabled under 65, or veterans with a 100 percent service-connected rating. The auditor's page put the tax year 2025 filing deadline at December 31, 2026.

  • Owner-occupancy reduction: 2.5 percent off for someone living in the house on January 1, requested on DTE 105C and frequently handled at transfer.
  • Current agricultural use value: a one-time $25 application fee, filed between the first Monday in January and the first Monday in March.
  • Recoupment: land taken out of farm use owes the tax savings of the preceding three years.

Buyers should ask the auditor which credits carry over, because the owner-occupancy reduction turns on the buyer's own residence.

What are the Lorain County transfer rules for a sale?

Conveyances reach the auditor in person or by e-file, and the postal service is out: mailed transfers ended on November 1, 2012. The desk works Monday through Thursday, shutting e-file intake at 3:00 p.m. and the counter at 4:00 p.m. Handwritten, incomplete or underpaid forms come back unprocessed. Staff cannot fill in conveyance forms or advise on them, citing Ohio Revised Code 4705.01, so paperwork preparation falls to a title company or lawyer.

Rental property adds a duty under Ohio Revised Code 5323.02: the owner names a contact agent to the auditor within 60 days of the conveyance filing, or risks a penalty of up to $150 on the parcel. A conveyance fee calculator on the auditor's site takes the sale amount and the number of parcels.

Which home improvements raise a Lorain County assessment?

The auditor's appraisal page separates upkeep from additions. Repairs that are not part of a complete modernization can be made without raising the tax. Exterior items on that list include painting, landscaping, new gutters, siding repair, storm windows, fencing and a replaced driveway. Interior items include rewiring, new plumbing, drywall repair, a replacement water heater and a furnace swapped for the same type.

These changes may add to the taxable value, according to the same page:

  • Fireplaces, new porches or decks, and room additions.
  • Added bathrooms, stall showers or other new plumbing fixtures.
  • Finishing an attic or basement.
  • A new or larger garage, and central air conditioning.
  • In-ground pools, and farm outbuildings, silos and grain bins.

An owner who tore down a dilapidated shed, garage or barn files a Razing Affidavit, DTE 26, so the building comes off the tax list. Filing it before a sale keeps a building that no longer stands from showing on the tax list.

Where does a Lorain County tax payment go?

Send it to the county treasurer, 226 Middle Avenue, Room 201, Elyria, or call 440-329-5787. The auditor sets values and takes no tax payments.

When is the next Lorain County reappraisal?

The next countywide reappraisal is 2030, per the Ohio Department of Taxation schedule. A triennial update comes first, in 2027.

What is the Inflation Cap Credit on Lorain County bills?

It is a credit applied automatically when school-related taxes rise faster than inflation after a reappraisal. It appears as INFLATION CAP CREDIT in the bill's Summary of Charges and comes from House Bill 186.

Can a Lorain County deed transfer go through the mail?

No, mailed transfers ended on November 1, 2012. Walk the conveyance form in on a Monday through Thursday before 4:00 p.m., or use an approved e-file vendor ahead of 3:00 p.m.

Does a Lorain County value dispute cost anything?

No fee applies, according to the auditor. The notarized complaint must be filed or postmarked by March 31.
