Lucas County by the numbers

Who runs Lucas County property tax?

Two county offices share the work, both at One Government Center in Toledo. The Auditor sets values, keeps the tax records, accepts Board of Revision complaints and takes homestead applications. The Treasurer mails the bills, collects payments and handles delinquent parcels. Reach the Auditor at 419-213-4406. The Treasurer is in Suite 500.

Lucas County takes in 596 square miles of northwest Ohio along Lake Erie and the Maumee River. Toledo serves as the seat and has the most residents, with Sylvania, Maumee, Oregon and Waterville as the other cities and Holland, Ottawa Hills and Whitehouse among the villages, per Wikipedia. The city or village and school district of your parcel shape its bill.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Lucas County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How is a Lucas County property tax bill calculated?

The Auditor's All About Property Taxes guide describes two steps. First, the property's market value is converted to a 35 percent assessed value. Second, that assessed value is multiplied by the tax rate for the taxing district and divided by 1,000.

The guide stresses that voters, not appraisers, set the rate through levies. As printed in its 2023 example, the rate for Sylvania city and Sylvania City School District was 82.695213, while Toledo city and Toledo City School District was 66.241870. The guide adds that Ohio taxes real property one year in the rear, so a bill paid in 2026 is for tax year 2025.

It also explains two older state credits. A 10 percent non-business credit and a 2.5 percent owner-occupied credit exist, but neither applies to levies passed after 2014, including replacement levies, so they do not cut the whole bill by those percentages. Look at your bill to see what credits it shows.

What are the Lucas County payment deadlines?

Each bill has two installments, with the due dates printed on it. The Treasurer's site states that the next due date is posted once bills are mailed. Under section 323.17, a delayed tax duplicate can push the payment dates to January 31 and July 20, which is why the dates can shift from year to year.

The Treasurer's site carries an important warning about mailing a payment. USPS postmarks can show a date a day or more after you mail, and Ohio law uses the postmark to decide whether a payment is on time. The office suggests three fixes:

  • Mail the check well ahead of the due date.
  • Ask for a hand-stamped postmark at the post office counter.
  • Pay online, which the site says is available at any time.

The Treasurer also lists a payment plan option on its home page. Ask that office for the terms before you fall behind.

How do I contest a Lucas County value?

Complaints go to the Board of Revision from January 1 through the end of March. On its Board of Revision page, the Auditor lists three board seats: Auditor, Treasurer and one Commissioner, or their delegates. Value is the only subject it hears. Rate and levy complaints are outside its reach.

The owner must prove the case. The Auditor's guide points to nearby comparable sales, your own recent purchase price or a private appraisal. For a house damaged or torn down, a separate DTE 26 application adjusts value starting the next tax year.

What happens to my tax while a complaint is pending?

You may pay based on your own figure. Section 5715.19 requires the Treasurer to accept a payment computed on the value stated in your complaint while the complaint is pending. If the final value turns out higher than what you paid, interest runs on the shortfall from the original due date, so keep the complaint number handy when you pay.

The statute sets other rules worth knowing before you file:

  • Filing is open until March 31 or the end of first-half collection, whichever is later.
  • The board has 180 days after the last filing day to rule.
  • A second complaint on a parcel in the same interim period needs a changed fact, such as a sale at arm's length, a casualty loss or a major improvement.
  • Hold nothing back: evidence you keep from the board may be barred on appeal.

Which Lucas County tax relief programs can a seller or heir use?

The Auditor's homestead exemption page describes four tracks. Owners aged 65 and up, plus owners who are totally and permanently disabled, can claim it for the home they live in if 2025 taxable income was $41,000 or less; Social Security does not count, but a spouse's taxable income does. Disabled veterans rated or compensated at 100 percent qualify without an income limit. Surviving spouses of first responders killed in the line of duty can qualify for an enhanced version.

For tax year 2025, payable in 2026, the page says the exempted value is $29,000, and that amount doubles for disabled veterans and the surviving spouses. The exemption comes off the taxable value of the primary residence only. Questions go to Homestead@co.lucas.oh.us or 419-213-4406.

When the home sells, Ohio's value statement asks the buyer to confirm with the seller whether the property carries these reductions or the agricultural use valuation, as section 319.202 requires. Be honest on that form, since a reduction may end with the sale.

What does the Lucas County housing market look like before a sale with tax owed?

Federal numbers on the QuickFacts page for Lucas County show 423,347 people as of July 2025 and 201,974 housing units. Between 2020 and 2024 the typical owned home was worth $163,900 and the typical household took in $62,224. Owners hold 62.0 percent of homes, and monthly gross rent was $934 at the median.

Deeds also pass through the Auditor before recording. The Auditor's transfer fact sheet prints $0.50 per parcel plus $4.00 for each $1,000 of price. Death, survivorship and own-trust transfers are generally exempt from the larger charge. Unpaid tax stays attached to the parcel, so get the Treasurer's balance for yours before signing a contract.

By what date must I contest a Lucas County value?

March 31. The Board of Revision accepts complaints from January 1 through March 31, and the Auditor says that window is set by Ohio law. State law allows the later date of March 31 or the close of first-half collection for the tax year.

Can the Lucas County Board of Revision lower my tax rate?

No. The Auditor states that the board hears appeals on property values only, not on the taxes themselves. Levy rates come from votes in your taxing district.

How do I prove a Lucas County value is wrong?

Bring evidence such as comparable neighborhood sales, a recent sale of the property or a private appraisal. The Auditor's guide says the burden of proof sits with the owner who files.

Who qualifies for the Lucas County homestead exemption?

Homeowners aged 65 or more, or totally and permanently disabled, who live in the house and had $41,000 or less in 2025 taxable income. Veterans rated 100 percent disabled and surviving spouses of first responders killed on duty also qualify, with a larger exempted amount.

Is a postmarked check still safe for a Lucas County tax payment?

Not always. The Treasurer warns that USPS postmarks can show a later date than the day you mail, and Ohio law uses the postmark date. Pay online or request a hand-stamped postmark.

Mahoning County by the numbers

Which Mahoning County offices handle a property tax bill?

A bill passes through three hands. The auditor sets each parcel's value and builds the tax list, the treasurer takes in payments, and the Board of Revision rules on disputes over value. Call the auditor at 330-740-2010 for forms and exemptions. The treasurer's counter is on the courthouse ground level at 120 Market Street, Youngstown, with phones at 330-740-2460 and weekday hours that end at 4:30 in the afternoon.

A county leaflet makes one point plainly: the auditor has no say over rates. Each school board, township, city and the county submits a budget, voters approve the levies, and the state tax department's procedures turn them into rates. An owner unhappy with a rate is told to attend budget hearings and write to those taxing bodies.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Mahoning County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What kind of housing market does Mahoning County have?

Mahoning County covers 425 square miles on Ohio's eastern edge, next to Pennsylvania. It was carved out of Trumbull and Columbiana counties and formed on March 1, 1846, with Youngstown as the seat and largest city. Census takers counted 228,614 people in 2020, and the 2025 estimate has slipped further to 224,706. Wikipedia notes the county has been losing people since about 1970.

Twenty public school districts divide the county, among them Youngstown City, Boardman, Canfield, Poland, Austintown, Struthers and Western Reserve. School levies drive much of a bill, so the district listed on the parcel record shapes what an owner pays.

QuickFacts figures for 2020 to 2024 describe a modestly priced market:

  • Typical value of a home that its owner lives in: $154,700
  • Share of homes occupied by owners: 70.3 percent
  • Gross rent at the midpoint: $791 a month
  • Households: 98,065, at 2.25 people each
  • Residents aged 65 and over: 24.4 percent

With nearly one resident in four past 65, the senior relief programs described below reach a large share of owners.

How does the auditor set value, and what caps the increase?

Under Ohio law the taxable amount is 35 percent of market value. The leaflet adds that every parcel is revalued on a six-year cycle, with appraisers checking exteriors each time. Market value means the price a willing seller would take from a willing buyer. Appraisers study sales and apply them to the property record, so a wrong bedroom count or a missing garage can raise a value without the owner noticing.

Two limits soften increases. A 1976 law, House Bill 920, grants a credit against voted millage so that a reappraisal does not raise what existing levies collect. A newer measure, House Bill 186, set up an inflation cap credit for certain property classes. Applying it meant a one-time mid-cycle rate change from the state, and the treasurer says any overpayment will be returned as a credit or refund.

Timing surprises sellers too. According to the auditor's FAQ, taxes are collected a year behind and a parcel is judged as it stood on January 1. A demolished garage may keep appearing on a bill, and a split or merger recorded this year reaches the tax list the year after.

When and how are Mahoning County taxes paid?

Bills arrive in two installments, and the treasurer's home page announces each deadline. The 2026 second-half deadline was September 18, a later date than usual because the new state credit held up bill production. The page adds that never receiving a bill does not erase the 10 percent late penalty, so an owner with no bill in hand should request a copy from the treasurer.

Ways to pay, as listed by the Mahoning County Treasurer
MethodWhat the treasurer's page says
OnlineCards, e-check, Apple Pay, Google Pay and Samsung Pay. Cards carry 2.5 percent with a $2.00 minimum, e-check carries $1.50

The treasurer also warns that a postmark often reflects the day a postal machine first handled the envelope, possibly days after you dropped it off. Paying electronically, mailing early, or requesting a hand-stamped mark at the retail counter avoids that risk.

How do I appeal a Mahoning County property value?

The route is a written complaint against the valuation, sent to the Board of Revision. Three officeholders sit on it by statute: the auditor, the treasurer and the commissioners' president, with two forming a quorum. Complaints are accepted from January until the end of March. For tax year 2025 the cutoff passed on March 31, 2026, and the 2026 round opens in early January 2027.

A hearing deals with value only. Rates and the size of the bill are outside its reach, and the person complaining has to make the case. The auditor's page suggests bringing:

  • A sale within the last 24 months, with the settlement statement and a notarized arm's-length affidavit
  • A tax-purpose appraisal from a certified appraiser
  • Photographs paired with professional repair estimates
  • Builder-certified costs for construction five years old or less

Feuds with neighbors, nearby pets, sewer trouble, and the fact that you never improved the property carry no weight. Send the form to the Board at the auditor's office or hand-deliver it. The Board takes no responsibility for lost mail, so keep following up until a date-stamped copy reaches you.

What tax relief can Mahoning County owners apply for?

Residential and farm parcels get a non-business credit with no paperwork. The owner-occupancy credit needs an application unless the owner already receives it. The auditor also describes:

  • Homestead Exemption. Open to resident owners who are 65 or older, permanently disabled, or a qualifying surviving spouse, within an income limit. That limit was $40,000 for tax year 2025 and moves to $41,000 for tax year 2026. The value shielded in 2025 was $29,000, doubling to $58,000 in the enhanced version for disabled veterans and surviving spouses of public service officers, which has no income test.
  • CAUV farm valuation. Tracts of ten acres or more used solely for commercial farming qualify, as does smaller land averaging $2,500 a year in sales. The auditor must receive the application between the first Monday of January and the first Monday of March; a postmark alone does not count.
  • Recoupment. Dropping out of CAUV triggers a charge equal to three years of taxes, a point any farm seller should raise with the auditor before closing.

The auditor's page also says the state updates CAUV soil values every three years, with the next change applying to tax year 2026.

What should a Mahoning County seller check on the tax account before closing?

Begin with the balance owed. Delinquent taxes are handled by the treasurer at 330-740-2460, so get a figure before a buyer signs. Charges levied by outside bodies, for example lighting or grass cutting, are folded into the tax breakdown. Mortgages, mechanic's claims and judgments never show on the bill. The recorder at 330-740-2345 and the Clerk of Courts at 330-740-2104 can speak to those.

Then prepare the deed. Land described in acres or part of a platted lot must first be reviewed at the GIS and Tax Map table, 21 West Boardman Street. The auditor's checklist also asks for the seller's marital status, the buyer's tax mailing address, a legal description and the prior deed reference. It prices a sale at $1.00 per $1,000 of price for the conveyance fee, $3.00 per $1,000 for the permissive fee and 50 cents a parcel to transfer, so have the auditor confirm the total.

Whatever shape the house is in, unpaid taxes will turn up in the title search, and the treasurer can settle them ahead of closing.

More questions about Mahoning County, OH Property Tax Guide

Which office answers questions about a Mahoning County bill?

The treasurer, at 330-740-2460, handles payments and balances. The auditor, at 330-740-2010, handles value, exemptions and forms. Both work from 120 Market Street in Youngstown.

When does the complaint window close each year?

On March 31, counted from the year after the tax year. Tax year 2025 complaints were due by March 31, 2026, and tax year 2026 complaints can be filed starting in early January 2027.

Can repair needs lower my valuation?

They can, when documented. Photographs plus a contractor's estimate are accepted, though the owner must show the value is too high. A general objection to higher taxes will fail.

Does the treasurer take credit cards?

Yes, online or by phone. The page shows a 2.5 percent card fee with a $2.00 floor and $1.50 per e-check payment, and these go to the payment vendor.

Does selling CAUV farmland trigger a penalty?

It may. The auditor states that withdrawing or no longer qualifying brings a penalty of three years of taxes. Acreage can stay enrolled if the new owner applies or the former owner renewed on time, so check with the auditor first.

Medina County by the numbers

Who collects property tax in Medina County, Ohio?

The Medina County Treasurer collects it, from the County Administration Building at 144 North Broadway in Medina. The phone number is 330-725-9748, and the counter is staffed from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays, with extended hours until 6:00 p.m. on a due date. The auditor values the parcels and handles exemptions, while the treasurer's website, separate from the auditor's, is where you look up a bill and pay it.

Bills are issued twice a year. If one never arrives, the treasurer suggests calling the office or using the Search and Pay Taxes link on its site, which lets you print an official bill to pay by mail or at the counter.

What is Medina County like, and what do homes cost?

Medina County covers 423 square miles in northeast Ohio, south and west of Cleveland, with Cuyahoga, Summit, Wayne, Ashland and Lorain counties as neighbors. It was created in 1812 and organized in 1818. Medina is the seat, Brunswick is the biggest city, and Wadsworth and part of Rittman are the other cities. Sharon Center and Valley City are census-designated places. The county park district manages 18 parks and trails across 6,353 acres.

The county has kept growing. The 2020 census counted 182,470 residents, up from 172,332 in 2010, and the 2025 estimate is 185,025. Westfield Insurance and the Cleveland Clinic's Medina hospital were the two largest employers in the county's 2020 financial report.

Census QuickFacts for 2020 to 2024 show the high end of Ohio's county markets:

  • Value of an owned home at the midpoint: $287,000
  • Share of homes lived in by owners: 80.3 percent
  • Household income at the midpoint: $94,968
  • Monthly cost for owners with a mortgage: $1,726
  • Gross rent at the midpoint: $1,143
  • Permits for new housing in 2025: 430

When were the 2026 Medina County bills due, and what do late payments cost?

The county's 2026 due dates were February 27 for the first half and August 28 for the second half. Both dates came later than in past years, when the treasurer's news archive shows deadlines in early or mid February and in July. The second-half bills were late because the county auditor had to reprogram software for a new state law. Every one of Ohio's 88 counties had delays.

Medina County 2026 installments as announced by the County Treasurer
InstallmentBills and amountDue date and penalties
First half, tax year 202578,728 bills mailed, $412,675,472 billed for the full yearDue February 27, 2026. A 5 percent penalty if postmarked after that date and 10 percent after March 9
Second half, tax year 202567,566 bills mailed August 6, $204,658,816 billedDue August 28, 2026. A 5 percent penalty after that date and 10 percent after September 7

The year in the left column is the tax year, which trails the calendar year in Ohio. Future due dates are announced in the treasurer's newsroom each time bills go out, so check there rather than assuming last year's dates.

How can I pay a Medina County tax bill?

The treasurer offers several routes, and the vendor fees go to the vendors, not to the county:

  • Online. E-check costs $1.50. Debit cards carry a 1.99 percent fee, and credit cards or a PayPal account carry 2.5 percent.
  • Phone. Call 1-888-607-8389 to pay by e-check or card, with the same fees.
  • Counter. Bring the whole bill to 144 North Broadway. Checks, cash and credit cards are accepted.
  • Drop boxes. Twenty-four hour boxes stand at the Treasurer's office, Brunswick City Hall on Center Road, the Lodi Library on Wooster Street and the Wadsworth Municipal Building on Maple Street. Include the bill stub with a check.
  • PayPal Credit. Its bill-me-later option spreads payment over six months with no interest, subject to credit approval and a 2.5 percent vendor charge. The treasurer says some taxpayers use it to meet the due date and avoid the 10 percent penalty.

Mail is riskier than it used to be. Since December 2025 the postal service has postmarked mail at regional facilities, so a postmark may not match the day you dropped the envelope in a box. The treasurer relies on the postmark and suggests mailing early or asking a post office counter to hand-stamp the envelope.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Medina County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What is the inflation cap credit on a Medina County bill?

It is a credit created by House Bill 186 that limits increases on certain unvoted school taxes to the rate of inflation. The treasurer says six of Medina County's eight school districts fell under the state's 20 mill floor: Black River, Brunswick, Buckeye, Cloverleaf, Highland and the Career Center. After the auditor's 2025 reappraisal raised values, those districts received more than $14 million in additional unvoted revenue. The cap sends about $5.5 million back to taxpayers, shown on the second-half bill as Inflation Cap Credit.

Not every owner receives it, since the treasurer says the change affected six of the county's eight school districts. If a second-half bill shows no credit and you think it should, ask the auditor's office about the parcel before assuming the bill is wrong.

What did the homestead change do for senior and disabled owners?

In December 2025 the Ohio legislature doubled the tax reduction for qualified homestead owners, and it first showed on first-half 2026 bills as a separate line called Local Homestead Reduction. The treasurer estimates about 11,500 of the county's 67,700 homeowners qualify. The reduction depends on the local millage, and in the two districts the treasurer checked it came to $354 in one township and $504 in another.

To qualify you must own and live in the home and meet one of these conditions:

  • Age 65 or older
  • Permanent and total disability
  • A veteran, or the spouse of a first responder killed in the line of duty

The treasurer cites an Ohio adjusted income limit of $41,000. Applications go through the County Auditor, whose office answers at 330-725-9754.

How do I contest a Medina County property value?

File a complaint with the Board of Revision, which hears appeals of auditor values. The form must be in the County Auditor's office, either postmarked or delivered, by March 31. The treasurer's newsroom warns that the new postmark practice affects this deadline too, so deliver the form by hand when you can.

Ask the auditor's office at 330-725-9754 for the current form before you file. The Board of Revision rules on the appraised value of the property. The levies that drive the bill are placed on the ballot by local taxing bodies, and a complaint cannot change them.

What should a Medina County seller check about taxes before closing?

Request a current balance from the treasurer at 330-725-9748 and look up the parcel through Search and Pay Taxes. Because Ohio bills a year in arrears, a sale in the first half of a year can leave the second-half installment for the prior tax year still unpaid. Ask the title company how that installment will be handled at closing, and compare its figure with the bill itself.

Also compare the parcel's school district with the credit list above and confirm whether a homestead reduction appears on the current bill. Whoever the buyer is, the treasurer's balance has to be cleared from the sale proceeds.

More questions about Medina County, OH Property Tax Guide

What number do I call for Medina County property taxes?

330-725-9748 reaches the County Treasurer. For homestead applications, call the County Auditor at 330-725-9754.

What were the 2026 due dates in Medina County?

February 27, 2026 for the first half and August 28, 2026 for the second half. A mailed payment had to be postmarked on or before those dates to avoid the 5 percent penalty.

How much is the late penalty?

The treasurer announced 5 percent for payments after the due date and 10 percent once a set later date passed, which was March 9 for the first half and September 7 for the second half in 2026.

Where can I drop off a check after hours?

Twenty-four hour drop boxes are at the Treasurer's office in Medina, Brunswick City Hall, the Lodi Library and the Wadsworth Municipal Building. Include the bill stub.

Is the Board of Revision deadline affected by postmarks?

Yes. The treasurer's newsroom notes that forms must be postmarked or physically in the auditor's office by March 31, and that postmarks may not show the day you mailed. Hand delivery avoids the risk.

Miami County by the numbers

What is Miami County, Ohio, made of?

Miami County belongs to the Dayton metropolitan area. Shelby County lies to the north, Champaign and Clark to the east, Montgomery to the south and Darke to the west. Organized in 1807 and named for the Miami people, it spans 410 square miles, according to Wikipedia. The auditor's home page counts 54,707 parcels.

Troy holds the courthouse and is the largest city. Piqua and Tipp City are cities too, and Huber Heights and Union each extend partly into the county. Troy, Piqua, Tipp City, Covington, Milton-Union, Miami East, Newton, Bradford and Bethel each have their own public school district. Which one serves a house decides several of the levies printed on its bill.

How many Miami County households own their homes?

QuickFacts, the Census Bureau's county table, reports 112,634 residents in July 2025, 3.5 percent more than at the 2020 base. The housing rows below draw on five years of survey data ending in 2024.

  • Nearly three in four households (73.4 percent) own, among 44,906 households in all.
  • The middle owner-occupied house is valued at $229,100.
  • Monthly owner costs run $1,453 with a mortgage and $549 without one.
  • Gross rent is $966 at the median.
  • Household income is $76,817 at the median.
  • Permits for 340 new units were issued in 2025, against 47,930 housing units overall.

Roughly one occupied home in four is rented, which makes tenant-occupied sales in Troy or Piqua a familiar case.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Miami County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How does the Miami County Auditor set a value?

The auditor explains that Ohio requires a full reappraisal every sixth year, plus an update at the midpoint, and that the taxable base is set at 35 percent of market value. A record for each parcel sits in the office and anyone may inspect it. Ask which year brings the next update.

The auditor cannot change a tax rate. Rates reflect budget requests by local governments and votes by residents, and a bill equals the rate times the valuation on the general tax list. Absent a vote, Ohio limits taxation to ten mills. Every levy beyond that was approved at the polls. Special assessments for ditches, paving, curbs, sidewalks, sewers or water lines show up as their own line on the bill.

What are the Miami County tax due dates and late penalties?

The treasurer collects real estate tax in two installments, February 14 and July 20, and the printed statement confirms the dates. A postmark on the due date counts as on time.

Miami County tax collection dates and penalties, from the treasurer's FAQ
ItemDetail

The treasurer works from the Safety Building, 201 W. Main Street in Troy, phone (937) 440-6045. Options include mail with the bill stub, a counter visit on weekdays between eight and four, and the night deposit box on the building's east side. Card payments go through an outside processor that adds 2.50 percent, and eChecks add a flat $1.99.

Owners who fell behind can ask the office about a delinquent payment contract. Ohio law also permits tax lien certificate sales under section 5721.32 of the Revised Code.

Which tax breaks can Miami County homeowners claim?

The auditor's pages describe several programs, nearly all filed through that office.

  • Owner occupancy credit: available if you own the house and treat it as your main home on the January 1 that starts the filing year. It reaches the dwelling plus one acre and is often completed during the transfer.
  • Non-business credit: limited to residential and farm levies that predate the November 2013 election.
  • Homestead exemption: for homeowners aged 65 and up, or permanently disabled, who live in the house. Filing opens the first Monday of January and closes the first Monday of June, and new applicants take an income test.
  • Surviving spouse of a public service officer: the auditor describes a $58,000 reduction with no income limit when the officer died in the line of duty.
  • Current agricultural use value: for ten or more acres in commercial farming, or smaller tracts averaging $2,500 a year in gross income, with filing from the first Monday of January to the first Monday of March.

Phone the auditor at (937) 440-5925 to learn the homestead income limit.

Where can a Miami County owner contest a valuation?

The Board of Revision takes valuation complaints. The auditor is its permanent secretary, joined by the treasurer and the commissioners' president. An owner submits DTE Form 1, the Complaint Against the Valuation of Real Property, to the auditor from January 1 through March 31.

The board then sends a decision or schedules a hearing. The state's tax department stresses that a complaint challenges the assessed value and cannot touch the millage rate, which comes from local governments and voters. It suggests gathering sales of similar homes, an independent appraisal or photographs. An appraisal strengthens a case but is optional.

What do Miami County mobile home and farm owners need to know?

Mobile homes follow their own calendar, with the first half due March 1 and the second July 31 per the treasurer's FAQ. County pages add that owners of manufactured homes register them with the auditor, who assesses each home yearly and bills twice a year. The revenue is shared among townships, cities and schools just as real estate tax is.

Farmland follows another path. The auditor administers the current agricultural use value program, which the Ohio Department of Taxation oversees through soil rate values. In a reappraisal year, applications may be taken all year. Leaving agricultural use can change how land is valued, so talk to the auditor before listing a farm tract.

What does a Miami County seller owe the auditor at transfer?

The auditor's conveyance notice sets $2.00 for each thousand dollars of price, plus 50 cents per parcel for transfer. A check must match the amount to the penny or the conveyance is not processed. Ordinary sales go in on DTE Form 100, and exempt transfers on Form 100 (EX). A fee calculator on the auditor's site gives an estimate.

The recorder, auditor and engineer jointly adopted conveyance standards, and ORC 317.114 has governed recorded documents since July 1, 2009. Before closing, get the tax payoff from the treasurer and find out from the closing agent how the current bill is shared. If the buyer will occupy the house, the owner occupancy application is frequently filed with the transfer.

Which day is the Miami County second installment due?

July 20, per the treasurer's FAQ. The February installment is due on the 14th, and the statement carries exact dates. A payment postmarked by the deadline counts as timely.

How much are late payment penalties in Miami County?

Five percent in the first ten days after the deadline, then 10 percent on unpaid current tax. The treasurer's office offers delinquent payment contracts.

January 1 through March 31, on DTE Form 1 filed with the county auditor. The Board of Revision then rules or schedules a formal hearing.

What fees go with a Miami County deed transfer?

The auditor lists $2.00 per thousand dollars of price and 50 cents per parcel, paid by a check for the exact amount. Use DTE Form 100, or Form 100 (EX) for an exempt transfer.

Where does a Miami County senior apply for the homestead exemption?

Apply at the auditor's office between the first Monday of January and the first Monday of June. Applicants need to be 65 or over, or permanently disabled, and live in the house. Call (937) 440-5925 about the income test.

Montgomery County by the numbers

Who sends and who sets a Montgomery County tax bill?

The work is divided between two offices, both at 451 West Third Street, Dayton, OH 45422. The Auditor sets values and runs appeals, and the Treasurer bills and collects. The Auditor can be reached at 937-225-4326, and the Board of Revision application can be requested at 937-496-6856.

Reach the Treasurer at 937-225-4010, weekdays 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.. Taxpayer Services is Option 1 on that line, and the delinquency specialists are Option 2. The county's Treasurer FAQ also lists a Semi-Annual Property Charge for solid waste services, with questions going to 937-224-8463.

What are the Montgomery County tax due dates?

Each year's halves fall due in February and July, and bills arrive in January and June. The 2026 dates, February 13 and July 24, are behind us. Per the Treasurer's paying page, a half that goes unpaid past its date draws a 10% penalty.

The county bills one entire year in arrears. The first-half bill covers January through June of the prior calendar year, and the second-half bill covers July through December of that year. Manufactured homes are billed in the actual calendar year instead, and their questions go to (937) 225-5255.

  • Paying the full year in February earns no discount. Differences between the halves are assessments, some of which appear only on the first-half bill.
  • When a mortgage servicer pays from escrow, let them know your bill arrived so they can ask the Treasurer for a copy.
  • A prepayment plan spreads taxes across monthly bills for owners with no past-due taxes, with enrollment at least 60 days before a half-year due date. Coupons go out at the start of March and August.

What is the 2026 reappraisal and when do new values start?

State law requires a full reappraisal in 2026, and the Auditor adjusts values from each property's grade, condition and style and from recent valid sales. The county's reappraisal FAQ says the new values take effect at the start of 2027 and show up in bills paid in 2027. They do not change the taxes paid during 2026.

Montgomery County 2026 reappraisal steps, per the Auditor's project timeline
WhenStep
July 2026Tentative value notices mailed
July and August 2026Informal review meetings by Zoom or phone
December 2026Final values go to the Department of Taxation for approval
January through March 2027Board of Revision window to appeal final values

Commercial values are set by use and neighborhood, and the county expects apartment, retail and office changes to vary widely. The informal review period has ended. The Property Owner Hotline is 937-224-8927 and Spanish assistance is 937-496-3260. A bigger value does not mean an equally bigger bill, since levies decide the tax rate, a point the FAQ makes with a 19% value rise.

How do you dispute a Montgomery County value?

A complaint filed with the Auditor's Board of Revision must arrive in the window that runs from early January through March 31. Each complaint is investigated and a formal hearing may follow. Proof falls on the owner, and the board may move a value up or down.

The county's reappraisal FAQ names the evidence that tends to help:

  • A record of an open-market sale of the property in the last three years.
  • An appraisal from the last three years.
  • Sales of comparable properties.
  • Photos or repair estimates that document condition problems.

The same FAQ says the Auditor only counts valid sales, meaning listings sold on the open market between a willing buyer and a willing seller. It sets aside sales between relatives, multi-property sales, sheriff's and bank sales, foreclosure auctions and quit-claim transfers. Rates move too: a value can also lead to a larger bill because a levy passed, and a property whose value fell can still see a higher bill if the effective tax rate went up.

Who qualifies for the Montgomery County homestead reduction?

According to the Treasurer's FAQ, the Homestead Reduction Program serves owners who are 65 or older and owners with a total and permanent disability, and the home must be their primary residence. The county's Homestead page carries the application details, so call the Auditor at 937-225-4326 with questions about income limits.

A sale triggers one more step. Under ORC 319.202, the buyer's value statement must either affirm that the seller reported no reduction or attach a sworn estimate of the reduction that both sides have accounted for. If you hold a homestead credit, tell your closing agent at the start.

How do you change a mailing address or prove what you paid?

Ohio law requires address changes for a tax bill to be submitted in writing to the Treasurer, and the county posts a Change of Address form for that purpose. Sellers who move out before closing should send it in so the next bill does not go astray.

Payment histories are not mailed automatically. If you pay through mortgage escrow, the amount withheld appears on the 1099 form from the lender. Without records of your own, call 937-225-4010, Option 1, and request an itemization of what was paid. To see how a bill is split among schools, townships and other districts, enter your parcel on the Auditor's site and open the Levy Distribution item, or call 937-225-4326.

What if Montgomery County taxes are late or a lien was sold?

The Treasurer offers delinquent payment plans. An owner who signs a monthly contract pays toward the new taxes while paying off the old ones, without additional interest and penalty. Start at the Treasurer's office or at 937-225-4010, Option 2.

A sold tax lien is different. The county says you cannot make payments on a sold lien through the Treasurer; you arrange payment with the company that bought it. To check release status, look in the Master Information section of the property record on the Treasurer's search page. If the page still reads lien sold, the lien has not been released, even if the holder was paid. Title examiners look for that line, so clear it before you list.

What does Montgomery County look like for owners and sellers?

Dayton anchors the county, which the 2020 census counted at 537,309 people, the fifth most in Ohio, in about 464 square miles, per Wikipedia. The county's FAQ puts the parcel count near 230,000.

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts shows 231,319 households averaging 2.24 people. Owners pay a median of $1,438 a month with a mortgage and $604 without one, and about 86% of residents stayed in the same house across a year. The county issued 1,079 building permits in 2025.

Use those figures as context when you read an escrow statement. Before closing, request the payoff on your parcel from the Treasurer and learn from your closing agent how a bill covering a prior year gets split.

When does the July installment come due in Montgomery County?

July is the month, and in 2026 the date was July 24. The first installment falls in February, and in 2026 that date was February 13.

What happens if a Montgomery County tax half is late?

A 10% penalty applies to either half left unpaid after its due date.

When is the deadline to dispute a Montgomery County value?

Complaints go to the Board of Revision from early January to March 31. For the new 2026 reappraisal values, the county says the window opens January 1, 2027.

Do I get a discount for paying a whole year of Montgomery County taxes in February?

No. The Treasurer says there is no discount for paying the full year at once, and the difference between the two halves comes from assessments.

Can I pay a sold tax lien at the Montgomery County Treasurer?

No. After a lien is sold you deal with the company that bought it, and you confirm the release when the parcel record stops showing lien sold.

Muskingum County by the numbers

Which two courthouse offices deal with Muskingum County tax bills?

Two courthouse offices share the work, and both sit at 401 Main Street in Zanesville. The auditor values property and runs the relief programs. The treasurer prints the bills and takes the payments.

The treasurer's FAQ says a new billing address must reach the office on a written, signed change-of-address form. Phone calls alone do not update it.

How does Muskingum County set the value of a house?

The auditor appraises every parcel, and Ohio law requires a full revaluation every six years. The auditor's revaluation FAQ says the most recent cycles were 2018 and 2024, and that the average value increase in the 2024 round was 36.135 percent. Rising sale prices over the preceding three years drove that jump.

A higher value does not translate one for one into a higher bill. The auditor explains that taxes depend on voter-approved levies and on the rates the Ohio Department of Taxation calculates from them. Rates for the coming year are not final until the end of December, and the auditor offers an online tax estimator in the meantime.

When can a Muskingum County owner challenge the value?

A formal complaint can be filed with the county auditor from January 1 through March 31. Under section 5715.19 the real deadline is March 31 or the close of first-half collection, whichever falls later. A mailed complaint counts as filed on its United States postmark, and a private meter mark does not count.

The complaint goes before the Board of Revision, made up of the auditor, the treasurer and one county commissioner or their representatives. The auditor also offers an informal review first. Evidence the auditor lists includes:

  • Sales of comparable homes.
  • An independent appraisal from within the past year.
  • Repair estimates for defects in the house.
  • Settlement documents from a recent purchase.
  • Income and expense statements for rentals.
  • Photographs.

While a complaint is pending, the owner may pay the amount computed on the value claimed in the complaint, and the treasurer accepts it. The statute adds that interest accrues if the final figure comes out higher.

What are the due dates and late charges on a Muskingum County tax bill?

Bills go out twice a year, in January or February and again in May or June, and the exact closing date is printed on each bill. The Revised Code's default installment dates are December 31 and June 20 under section 323.12, and the treasurer's schedule can differ. The auditor's FAQ showed first-half bills due February 14, 2025 and second-half bills due June 13, 2025.

The treasurer's FAQ describes the penalty as 10 percent of the current tax, cut to 5 percent when payment arrives within ten days of the due date. Interest is added on prior delinquencies each July 1 and on unpaid current taxes each December 1. Not receiving a bill does not waive the penalty.

Payment options include the online portal, a phone system at (833) 505-4134, a lobby kiosk and the counter at the Treasurer's Office. Electronic payments carry a processing fee, and the office does not take cards at the window.

What tax relief programs exist in Muskingum County?

The auditor lists three programs on its site, each with an application on file at the office.

  • Owner Occupancy Credit. A 2.5 percent cut on qualifying levies, open to anyone who owns the house and makes it their primary residence.
  • Homestead Exemption. The page describes it as a break for seniors aged 65 and up and for permanently and totally disabled owners: $29,000 of market value is shielded for tax year 2025, and applicants must fall under a $41,000 income limit. Disabled veterans and certain surviving spouses get a $58,000 exemption.
  • Current Agricultural Use Valuation. Farmland with at least ten acres in commercial agriculture can be taxed on soil rates. Smaller tracts qualify if they meet the $2,500 income test.

The auditor also announced that House Bill 479 would add roughly $475 of Homestead savings on the bill received in 2027, and that House Bill 186 created an Inflation Cap Credit applied to school levies for tax year 2025.

What happens to property tax when a Muskingum County house is sold?

Taxes follow the parcel, not the person, according to the treasurer. The treasurer's FAQ also says a bill for the full year goes to whoever is the owner of record, and that the seller should credit the buyer on the closing statement for the share of the year the seller owned. Ask your title agent to show that proration line.

Unpaid taxes complicate a sale. The treasurer states that they are a lien that can hinder or reduce a sale because the new owner inherits the delinquency. One year after certification as delinquent, the county prosecutor can file foreclosure, which adds penalties, interest and court costs and ends in a sheriff's sale. Muskingum County does not sell tax liens. Owners who also occupy the house can ask the treasurer about a written delinquency contract that spreads the balance over installments.

The statement of value filed with the deed also asks the seller about owner-occupancy reductions and farm-use valuation. Answer it carefully, because land that stops qualifying for farm-use valuation can face a recoupment charge.

What does Muskingum County look like for a seller?

Zanesville holds the courthouse, and the Muskingum River nearly bisects the county. The county covers 673 square miles and counted 86,410 residents in 2020. Its 2025 estimate is 87,014, a gain of 0.7 percent over the 2020 base, per the Census QuickFacts table.

The same table gives a $182,200 median value for owner-occupied homes and a $1,300 monthly housing outlay for owners who carry a mortgage, 2020 to 2024. Renters hold a bit under a third of occupied homes, and the median gross rent listed is $833. Seven public and parochial high schools serve the county, and Muskingum University and Zane State College keep a steady student and staff population in the housing market.

What should an owner do after a Muskingum County revaluation notice?

Start by looking up the parcel on the auditor's real estate search, which shows the tentative value under the Values heading, then compare it with recent sales of similar houses nearby. The auditor reports that value changes from the informal review period were posted to its website on October 25, 2024, so earlier changes are already reflected in what you see.

If the number still looks wrong, you have two routes. The informal review is a conversation with the appraisal staff, and the auditor says evidence is not required for it but that you are unlikely to see an adjustment without significant supporting documents. The formal route is the Board of Revision complaint, which is also where sellers and buyers raise a recent sale price. Because the complaint window closes each March 31, a seller who closes in the spring should ask whether a complaint is already pending, since the outcome can change the tax bill the new owner inherits.

The auditor also clarifies that it does not choose to raise or lower taxes. Voters approve or reject levies, and the state turns those levies and the total value of each district into tax rates.

Who sends Muskingum County property tax bills?

The Muskingum County Treasurer does. Bills are mailed in January or February and again in May or June, and you can reach the office at 401 Main Street in the county seat.

By when must a Muskingum County value complaint be filed?

March 31. The auditor accepts Board of Revision complaints from January 1 through March 31, and state law extends that to the close of first-half collection if later.

How big is the late charge on a Muskingum County bill?

Ten percent of the tax then due; the treasurer's FAQ cuts it to five percent when payment lands inside ten days after the deadline. Delinquent balances also pick up interest.

Who pays property tax at a Muskingum County closing?

Both sides share it by proration. The treasurer says the seller credits the buyer on the closing statement for the seller's portion, and the buyer then pays the bill when it comes due.

Does Muskingum County sell tax liens?

No. The treasurer states that the county does not sell tax liens. After taxes are certified delinquent for one year, the prosecutor can file a foreclosure action that ends in a sheriff's sale.

Portage County by the numbers

Who bills and collects property tax in Portage County, Ohio?

Two offices in Ravenna split the work. Valuation and rate-setting sit with the auditor. Billing and cash receipts sit with the treasurer, a separately elected office. A third body, the Board of Revision, hears valuation complaints, and the auditor acts as its secretary.

The county's own About Portage County page describes the auditor as the tax assessor for every political subdivision in the county and the treasurer as the collector of all tax money. It also says the treasurer sits on the Board of Revision. Sorting your question first saves a wasted call: what the house is worth goes to the auditor, and what is owed goes to the treasurer.

The auditor's real estate search site, portagecountyauditor.org, offers parcel searches and a tax estimator by taxing district and property value. Look your parcel up before listing, because the value shown there is what a buyer's agent opens first.

How is a Portage County tax bill figured?

The treasurer's tax rates page lays out the steps. The sequence runs from fair market value, to 35% of that as assessed value, to assessed value times the total mills over 1,000. Every Ohio owner carries a base of 10 mills from the state constitution, and voter-approved levies for schools, roads, libraries and other services stack on top.

Special assessments, such as water lines, sewer lines and storm water systems, are added after that. Reduction credits come off the total last. Rates are recalculated every year, and the page links the published rate sheets for 2010 through the 2025 rates collected in 2026.

  • The page defines fair market value as the figure a buyer and seller would settle on in an arm's length deal on the open market.
  • Assessed value in Ohio is 35% of that figure.
  • Total mills vary by taxing district, so two houses in one county can carry different rates.
  • Special assessments are billed in addition to the base tax.

The page lists the auditor's office at 330-297-3561 for questions about how rates are calculated. Use that number if your sheet and your bill do not match.

When are Portage County property taxes due?

The treasurer's page says taxes are collected twice a year, with about half due in February and the rest due in July. The July half is not always fixed on the calendar. In 2026 the Ohio Tax Commissioner moved the second-half deadline to September 9, because the new inflation cap credit under House Bill 186 delayed bill processing, and a county release said no interest or penalty would run before that date. That date has passed.

Read the due date printed on your own bill, since the state can move a deadline.

Missing a date costs money. R.C. 323.121 adds a 10% penalty to any half that is still unpaid after its final date. Pay the whole amount inside ten days of that date and the treasurer waives half of the penalty. Interest on delinquent balances follows at the statutory rate. A half still open when you sell should be settled out of your proceeds, so tell the title company early.

Can I appeal a Portage County valuation before I sell?

Yes, but only inside a fixed window. The county's answer on disputed values sets the auditor's intake from January 1 to March 31, and the Board of Revision hears what comes in. Mail goes to P.O. Box 1217, Ravenna, OH 44266, and has to arrive by March 31.

The county's instruction sheet adds details that trip up owners:

  • The signature on the DTE 1 complaint form must be notarized, or the Board will not take it.
  • The Board looks at the current tax year only, not earlier years.
  • A complaint built on a sale has to show an arm's length deal. The sheet says foreclosure sales, sheriff sales, bank transactions and sales between family members are generally not treated as valid.
  • High taxes alone are not grounds, because the Board weighs value, not the bill.
  • Filing does not excuse payment on time. You may pay on your claimed value while the case is open, but interest runs on any gap.

If the stated change in assessed value is at least $17,500, the school board gets 30 days to file a counter-complaint, and no hearing is set until that time passes. The governing statute is R.C. 5715.19. It limits repeat complaints within one interim period, with exceptions for an arm's length sale, a casualty loss, a major addition or a 15 percent occupancy swing.

Which Portage County offices will I deal with in a sale?

A closing here touches the auditor, the treasurer and the recorder. The table gathers what each one printed for the public.

Portage County offices involved in a home sale, with details as published on the county and auditor sites
OfficeRolePublished contact
AuditorTransfers the deed, keeps values, takes valuation complaints449 South Meridian Street, Ravenna; appraisal (330) 297-3568; main (330) 297-3565
TreasurerBills and collects both halvesReached through the county site, portagecounty-oh.gov
RecorderRecords the deed and mortgage releasesMain office (330) 297-3553; fax (330) 297-7349

Under the auditor's transfer page, deeds pass through the real estate department before recording. The listed charge is four dollars for each $1,000 of price plus fifty cents a parcel, filed on form DTE 100. Ohio also lets a county adopt a grantor-paid transfer tax capped at 30 cents per $100 (R.C. 322.02). Ask the auditor whether one is in force on your deed.

What is Portage County like for a seller?

Portage County sits in Northeast Ohio, with Ravenna as county seat and Kent as the largest city. Wikipedia names Kent, Ravenna, Aurora and Streetsboro as its cities, adds 18 civil townships, and puts the 2020 population at 161,791. The county covers 504 square miles, and 38% of residents live in rural areas.

The county's about page names Kent State University, Hiram College and Northeast Ohio Medical University among its schools, and it notes that Interstate 80, which includes the Ohio Turnpike, and Interstate 76 cross the county. In the same entry, 68.9% of occupied homes are lived in by their owners and 31.1% are rented.

Where your parcel sits changes the bill. A house in a city, a village school district or an unincorporated township carries a different mix of levies, so compare the rate sheet for your district rather than a countywide average.

What should a seller with back taxes ask for?

Start with a payoff request. Request a written payoff from the treasurer that shows each delinquent year with its penalty and interest, then hand it to the closing agent. Ask the auditor whether any special assessment is attached, since those travel with the parcel.

  • Request a printout of the parcel's tax history from the auditor's real estate site.
  • Ask the treasurer whether a payment plan is open on the parcel.
  • Settle with the title company who covers the half now accruing, you or the buyer.
  • Check for open valuation complaints, because a pending one can change what is owed.

An owner who cannot clear the debt before a traditional listing still has a route. A buyer paying cash can purchase the house in its present condition, with the tax satisfied out of the price when the sale closes.

Where do I file a property value complaint in Portage County?

Use the DTE 1 form and send it to the auditor at 449 South Meridian Street in Ravenna during January through March. The Board of Revision hears it, and the signature on the form must be notarized.

What is the assessed value of a house in Portage County?

The treasurer's rate page sets it at 35% of fair market value. Mills for your district are applied to that figure and the result is divided by 1,000.

Are Portage County tax bills paid in two parts?

Yes, in two installments: about half in February and the balance in July. The 2026 second half was moved to September 9, which is behind us, so trust the date on your own bill.

What does Portage County charge to transfer a deed?

Four dollars for each $1,000 of price, and fifty cents a parcel, as the auditor publishes. The recorder's fee is separate and follows R.C. 317.32.

Can I sell a Portage County house that owes taxes?

Yes. Whatever is owed comes out of your sale proceeds at closing, so obtain the treasurer's payoff figure before you sign anything. The debt does not have to be paid before an as-is contract is written.

Richland County by the numbers

Who values and who collects property tax in Richland County, Ohio?

In Richland County one office decides what each parcel is worth (the auditor) and another sends bills and posts the money (the treasurer). Find them in the same Mansfield building, 50 Park Avenue East, ZIP 44902, open weekdays 8am to 4pm. The auditor's number is 419-774-5501 and the treasurer's number is 419-774-5622.

A third body, the Richland County Board of Revision, hears complaints about value. Its three statutory members are the auditor, the treasurer and the chair of the board of county commissioners, and each can appoint a stand-in. For a seller the split is easy to remember. Value, exemption and complaint questions belong with the auditor. Balances, payment contracts and delinquency belong with the treasurer.

  • Auditor, 419-774-5501: valuation, Board of Revision complaint forms, owner occupancy and homestead applications, CAUV farmland.
  • Treasurer, 419-774-5622: bills, payments, payment contracts on real estate, and conveyance fee payments.
  • Sheriff's civil section, 419-774-3570: tax foreclosure and bank foreclosure sales.
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Richland County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What does the Richland County housing market look like on paper?

Land area is 495.23 square miles, and Mansfield, the seat, anchors the Mansfield metropolitan area. Lawmakers created Richland in 1808 and it was organized in 1813; Ashland County later took its eastern townships in 1846. It holds four cities (Mansfield, Ontario, Shelby and part of Galion), villages such as Bellville, Lexington and Shiloh, and 18 townships.

Owners live in about 68 of every 100 homes, while the 2020 census placed two thirds of residents in urban areas. The figures below show the scale of the local housing stock.

Census Bureau figures for Richland County, Ohio (population on July 1, 2025; other rows 2020-2024)
MeasureRichland County
Population estimate124,893

Source: QuickFacts table for Richland County.

When does Richland County revalue property again?

The auditor's page says the county's triennial update falls in tax year 2026, with the resulting bills payable in 2027. Ohio reappraises on a six-year cycle and updates values at the three-year midpoint without a physical inspection.

The auditor also summarizes three state reforms enacted in late 2025. House Bill 186 adds an inflation cap credit for districts at the 20-mill floor, and where it applies it shows up as a separate line on the bill. House Bill 335 holds inside millage growth to the rate of inflation in reset years. House Bill 129 changes the floor calculation beginning in tax year 2026. The auditor stresses that none of this ends property tax or freezes values.

How do I file a Board of Revision complaint in Richland County?

File the complaint form with the Richland County Auditor, 50 Park Avenue East in Mansfield. The county page gives January 2 through March 31 as the filing period and charges no fee. The statute, section 5715.19, allows filing until March 31 or the end of first-half collection, whichever is later, and counts the mailing postmark.

The county suggests calling the auditor before filing, because a flawed complaint can be dismissed. Keep these points in mind.

  • One complaint per parcel in a triennial period, unless the property sold, suffered a casualty or lost income. A complaint that was withdrawn still counts as the filing for that period.
  • Parcels can share a form only when they are contiguous or one economic unit, in the same taxing district, with identical ownership. When in doubt, file separately.
  • Attach the supporting documents you plan to use at the hearing when you file.
  • Hearing notice comes by certified mail at least 10 days out, and the hearing takes place in the auditor's office.

If the Board's written opinion still feels wrong, the next stops are the State Board of Tax Appeals and common pleas court.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Richland County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What evidence does the Richland County Board of Revision accept?

The person filing carries the burden of proof. The county's list of acceptable evidence reads like a checklist: comparable sales, a fee appraisal, itemized repair estimates, the closing statement and purchase contract after a recent sale, and income and expense records for rentals. Outcomes range from an increase to a decrease to no change.

Two limits matter to sellers. Sheriff's sales, bank sales, short sales and any sale where buyer or seller faced unusual pressure are not treated as arm's length, so they do not count as comparables. The Board also has no power over the tax rate, the percentage increase in a bill, the CAUV formula or the dollar amount of a bill, so a complaint that only objects to a higher bill goes nowhere.

Which tax reductions can a Richland County homeowner claim?

State tax officials describe three common programs, all handled through the auditor. Owner occupancy credit goes to the house you own and use as your main residence on January 1 of the filing year. Homestead exemption reaches owners aged 65 and up, owners with a permanent and total disability, and some surviving spouses. Most face an income test, but service-connected disabled veterans do not. Ohio House Bill 96 of 2025 also lets county commissioners adopt a local-option homestead exemption equal to the state amount, which applies without a separate application if the county turns it on. Ask the Richland County Auditor whether that local option is in place.

Farmland has its own track. Current agricultural use value, or CAUV, lets qualifying land be taxed on its farm value rather than market value. Ohio sets the qualifying bar at ten acres of commercial farming, or a smaller tract earning at least $2,500 a year in gross farm income on average. The county's CAUV page says the formula averages seven years of data with the high and low years dropped.

Farm sellers should note that the buyer's conveyance statement must say whether the land carried CAUV status, and leaving the program can bring a recoupment charge.

How are Richland County taxes paid, and what if I am behind?

Besides real estate, the treasurer takes personal property, mobile home and estate tax, and online card or eCheck payments carry a service fee. Real estate payment contracts exist for prepaying and for catching up. Ohio's default dates are December 31 and June 20, which counties may extend, and your bill shows the dates that apply.

A missed installment draws a ten percent penalty under section 323.121, and half of it is waived when the full amount arrives within ten days. Interest then accrues on delinquent taxes. The treasurer's page states that the delinquent tax collector works with the county prosecutor on foreclosures, which is why an unpaid parcel can move from a bill to a court case.

While a valid delinquent tax contract holds, interest stops, and a breach brings back the interest that was paused. If you hold a contract and plan to sell, get the payoff in writing from the treasurer first.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

What happens when a Richland County parcel reaches a tax foreclosure sale?

Tax foreclosure sales, when scheduled, are held on Friday mornings at 10:00 in the training room of the Sheriff's Office at 597 Park Avenue East in Mansfield. The sheriff advertises each parcel in a newspaper beginning three weeks before the first sale, reads withdrawals aloud at the start of the sale, and requires the winning bidder to pay in full at the sale. A parcel that draws no sufficient bid can be offered again two weeks later at the same minimum price.

Bank foreclosure sales follow a separate path. To comply with Ohio House Bill 390, they are conducted only online through the sheriff's auction site, and the sheriff recommends that first-time bidders finish the site's training well before an auction. Separately, the Land Bank (lower level 1 of the courthouse building) acquires vacant, abandoned houses to reduce blight.

An owner facing a tax judgment should call the treasurer's office at 419-774-5622 before the sale date to ask what payment, contract or sale the county will accept.

How do I sell a Richland County house when taxes are still owed?

Get a written balance from the treasurer, then check it against the auditor's parcel record for the legal description, owner name and mailing address. The buyer's statement filed with the auditor discloses whether a tax reduction or CAUV status applied, and the seller covers the conveyance fee and any county transfer tax before the recorder sees the deed.

Line up three items early: the treasurer's payoff, the auditor's conveyance paperwork and tax map pre-approval for the deed.

More questions about Richland County, OH Property Tax Guide

Which office answers questions about a Richland County tax bill?

The treasurer, at 419-774-5622, answers questions on amounts owed and payment contracts. The auditor, at 419-774-5501, handles value, exemptions and complaints. Both sit at 50 Park Avenue East in Mansfield.

When can a Richland County owner dispute a valuation?

From January 2 through March 31 each year, filed with the auditor at no charge, per the county page. The statute lets the deadline run later when first-half collection closes after March 31.

Is 2026 a revaluation year in Richland County?

Yes. The county auditor says the triennial update occurs in tax year 2026, with taxes payable in 2027. State changes from House Bills 186, 335 and 129 are tied to those reset years.

Can selling the house stop a Richland County tax foreclosure sale?

Possibly, but ask first. Call the treasurer at 419-774-5622 for the judgment payoff and confirm timing with the sheriff's civil section at 419-774-3570.

Where is a Richland County deed recorded after a sale?

File it with the Richland County Recorder at 50 Park Avenue East in Mansfield. The recorder accepts deed transfers electronically but asks that tax map pre-approval be included. Documents that need tax map and auditor review must be brought to the courthouse in person.

Ross County by the numbers

What is Ross County, Ohio, like for a home seller?

Ross County sits in Appalachian Ohio, hilly and mostly rural, with Chillicothe as its seat and its one city. The territorial governor proclaimed it on August 20, 1798, the sixth county of the Northwest Territory, and only Ashtabula County has more land area in Ohio. Paint Creek meets the Scioto River southeast of Chillicothe, and the Scioto itself flows south through the east-central part of the county.

Beyond the city sit villages including Adelphi, Bainbridge, Clarksburg, Frankfort, Kingston and South Salem, plus 16 townships. Eleven school districts reach into the county, among them Chillicothe City, Huntington Local, Paint Valley Local, Southeastern Local, Zane Trace Local, Adena Local and Waverly City. Ohio University runs a regional campus in Chillicothe.

The July 1, 2025 Census estimate is 76,429 residents, with 32,165 housing units. Owners live in 69.6% of homes. An owner-occupied home has a median value of $171,500, rent runs $906 at the median, and the middle household earns $61,303. Workers average 26.4 minutes getting to work, against 21.8 in Richland County, which suits a county of 689 square miles and about 112 people per square mile.

Who bills and who values property in Ross County?

Valuation sits with the auditor, and billing and collection sit with the treasurer. The treasurer's office is in the Ross County Courthouse at 2 North Paint Street, Suite F, Chillicothe, Ohio 45601, and the phone is 740-702-3080, the same number the treasurer's pages give for auditor questions. The email for the treasurer is treasurer@rosscountyohio.gov. The auditor runs an online parcel search and a tax estimator on its own site.

Ross County's Board of Revision combines the treasurer, the auditor and the commissioners' president. A complaint is filed at the auditor's office, which passes it to the Board.

Ross County bills reflect values set a year earlier. Ross County collects a year behind, so money paid in 2026 settles the 2025 tax year. Ohio requires a full reassessment at least once in six years plus a midpoint update.

What is the Ross County billing calendar, and what does a late payment cost?

On the treasurer's collection page, first-half 2026 payments were due February 20 and second-half payments August 21; a weekend or holiday due date moves to the next business day. Both of those dates have passed. Mailings go out in mid-January and again in mid-June or early July. Contact the treasurer's office for the 2027 dates. Section 323.12 of the Revised Code names December 31 and June 20 as the baseline, subject to county extension.

The table gathers the penalty and deadline rules that matter most to a seller.

Ross County Treasurer and Auditor rules on penalties and deadlines
ItemRule
Late payment received within 10 calendar days5% penalty
Any later payment10% penalty
Prior-year taxes carried overInterest charged August 1
All past-due taxesInterest charged December 1
Delinquent list publicationPay or sign a contract by October 31 to stay off the auditor's list
Owner occupancy applicationJanuary 1 to the first Monday in June
Valuation complaintJanuary 1 to March 31

Source: Ross County Treasurer FAQ and Reducing Your Taxes pages.

The postmark decides whether a mailed payment is timely, and the treasurer cautions that it often records first processing, which can come after drop-off. Mail early. Anyone whose earlier payment failed to clear must pay by cash, cashier's check or money order.

What tax relief can Ross County homeowners apply for?

The owner occupancy credit takes a reduction off the home site and the house for owners who live there as a principal residence. Applications are accepted at the auditor's office between January 1 and the first Monday in June. Excluded: rentals, corporate or partnership owners, units inside retail or commercial buildings, depreciation-taxed manufactured homes, and land past the first acre.

The homestead exemption is run through the same office. The Ohio Department of Taxation lists the reduction for a low-income senior or disabled owner at $29,700 of home value for tax year 2026 real property, with an income threshold of $41,000 for that year. The bigger figure, $59,400, covers disabled veterans and widowed spouses of public service officers killed on duty, and carries no income test. The credit equals the tax charged on that slice of value, so a higher local rate means a larger credit. A real property application has to be filed by the last day of the tax year.

  • Penalty remission: request it from the treasurer on Form 23A, and only for reasons Ohio law allows.
  • Military extension: National Guard and reserve members called to active duty, or a spouse or dependent parent applying for them, can get up to five years to pay without penalty or interest.
  • Monthly Budget Pay Plan: a free service that lets owners pay a little each month toward the next bill.

What is the route for disputing a Ross County valuation?

An owner who disputes the auditor's number files with the auditor's office from January 1 to March 31. If first-half collection ends after March 31, section 5715.19 uses that later day, and mail is dated by postmark. The Board must give ten days' notice of the hearing and decide within 180 days of the filing cutoff.

Ross County's treasurer points to the recent sale price, documented by closing papers, as the best proof. A house that has not sold lately needs comparable sales instead, and condition photos can help. The same section limits repeat complaints on one parcel within an interim period. A second filing needs a new event: a sale at arm's length, casualty damage, a big improvement or a 15 percent occupancy swing.

A pending complaint lets the owner tender tax computed on the claimed value, and the treasurer is directed to take it.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Ross County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What are Ross County's options for delinquent taxes?

The treasurer offers two plans meant to keep owners out of foreclosure. A Delinquent Tax Contract splits back taxes into five equal installments, with the first due at signing and the rest added to the next four February and July bills. A SMART Payments plan folds current taxes and past-due taxes into one monthly payment that can run 30 months or longer. Under both, no new interest or penalty is added once the contract is signed and the first payment is made, but missing a payment cancels the contract and the stopped charges return. If legal action has already begun, a court cost is added to the first payment.

The treasurer's FAQ says the auditor publishes the delinquent tax list and recommends paying or signing a contract by October 31 to avoid publication. It also says there is no fixed date by which a property is foreclosed, and that the office will work with owners who are struggling.

What did the 2025 and 2026 state reforms change in Ross County?

The treasurer's site summarizes five property tax bills signed in late 2025 and early 2026. One changes how sales ratio studies pick the sales used in valuation. One revises the 20-mill floor calculation. One creates an inflation cap credit for school districts at the floor, and the treasurer states that all of the county's school districts sit at the 20-mill floor, with the credit showing up only in the second-half 2026 collection. One lets county budget commissions trim levies judged unnecessarily high. One caps growth in inside millage at the rate of inflation during reappraisals and triennial updates.

How do I handle property tax when selling in Ross County?

A tax bill can reach a new owner after closing because the tax follows the parcel. According to the treasurer, the buyer usually receives a prorated credit in the closing papers, so read the settlement statement closely. Request the balance in writing and ask whether a delinquent tax contract is open.

The auditor endorses the deed before recording. The buyer's value statement covers tax reductions and CAUV farm status, and the seller pays the conveyance fee plus any county transfer tax. Under section 322.02 the county rate can reach thirty cents per hundred dollars of value, so ask the Ross County Auditor which rate applies.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

More questions about Ross County, OH Property Tax Guide

What were the Ross County tax due dates in 2026?

Collections in 2026 fell due February 20 and August 21. Ask the treasurer at 740-702-3080 for the next pair of dates.

How much is the late charge in Ross County?

Five percent when received within ten calendar days, ten percent after that. Interest on carried-over tax begins August 1, and December 1 applies it to everything past due.

Until when can a Ross County owner contest a valuation?

File at the auditor's office from January 1 through March 31. If first-half collection closes after that, state law extends the window.

Can I avoid the Ross County delinquent tax list?

Yes, by paying or signing a contract with the treasurer by October 31. The office says the payment has to be received, not just postmarked, before the auditor's cutoff.

Which office records the deed after a Ross County sale?

The Ross County Recorder, at 2 North Paint Street, Suite E in Chillicothe, phone 740-702-3000. The auditor must endorse the deed first.

Scioto County by the numbers

Which Scioto County offices deal with property tax?

Three county offices share the work, all at 602 7th Street in Portsmouth. The Scioto County Auditor, Room 103 at 740.355.8264, sets values, takes complaints and processes homestead forms. Weekday hours run 8:00 am to 4:30 pm. The Scioto County Treasurer (Room 102, phone (740) 355-8272) sends the bills and collects the money. The Scioto County Recorder, in Room 110, handles the deed last.

The treasurer's office describes itself as part of the county's check and balance system with the auditor. In practice that means you ask the auditor why a value changed and ask the treasurer what you owe and when. Both offices are reachable by phone, and the treasurer's website has a Pay Online page for bills.
