How much did the latest triennial update change Scioto County values?

In its latest triennial update, required every three years, the auditor reports an average countywide value increase of about 26.4 percent. Under state rules, the auditor says, values must stay within 90 to 110 percent of what homes sell for, tested against three years of sales, and strong price gains forced the increase.

The auditor adds that state reviewers rejected the first set of tentative values and required resubmission using values deemed sufficient for approval. Values come from sales data, market trends and statistical analysis, not from a physical inspection of every house. Averages hide big swings between parcels, so check your own record against nearby sales.

Farmland owners should know that current agricultural use value rates are reset in a triennial year by the state, not by the auditor.

What is the Inflation Cap Credit on a Scioto County tax bill?

The auditor explains that House Bill 186 introduced an "Inflation Cap Credit" for qualifying school district levies. It prints on the bill as a separate line, and parcel-specific inputs make the amount differ from one house to the next.

  • If you paid your second-half bill before the credit was applied, you need not do anything.
  • Any overpayment carries forward and is applied to the next first-half bill.
  • Homeowners who pay through an escrow account at a lender need no action, according to the treasurer, who said it was working directly with lenders.

The state's implementation work delayed the second-half bills that year. As a result, second-half real estate and manufactured home taxes for 2026 were due August 20, which has passed.

What are the Scioto County due dates, and what happens after them?

The statute (R.C. 323.12) allows one payment by December 31 or two installments, the second by June 20. A payment is timely when the treasurer has it by the last day, or when the envelope bears a U.S. Postal Service postmark dated that day or earlier. Postage-meter marks from a private machine are not accepted.

The county can move a date, as it did for the 2026 second half. Always read the due date printed on your bill instead of assuming the statutory one.

Late payment rules from R.C. 323.12 and 323.121, Ohio Revised Code
EventWhat the statute says
First half unpaid after its due dateTen percent added to what remains of that half
Second half unpaid after its due dateA like 10 percent penalty on the balance of unpaid current taxes

If you cannot pay, call the treasurer early and ask about a delinquent tax contract before the penalties build.

How do I challenge my Scioto County property value?

The complaint goes to the auditor. R.C. 5715.19 lets you file through March 31 of the next year at a minimum, and longer if first-half collection closes after that date. The auditor hands each filing to the board of revision, and a mailed one is dated by its postmark.

The auditor also invites owners who believe the market value is wrong to file a complaint form with supporting evidence. Good evidence includes:

  • a recent appraisal or closing statement for your own home
  • sales of similar nearby houses
  • repair estimates that show a defect lowering value
  • photos or a report of damage from a casualty

A repeat filing has a limit. Filing twice on one parcel in the same interim period is barred. Four later events lift the bar: an arm's length sale, a casualty loss, a substantial improvement, or occupancy moving by fifteen percent or more.

Who qualifies for the Scioto County homestead exemption?

The auditor's page describes a state-funded break for homeowners who reach 65 in the year they first apply, or who are permanently and totally disabled. Applicants must own the house and call it their main residence as of January 1, and stay inside the state's income limits. The auditor offers separate forms for older owners, disabled owners, veterans, and the surviving spouse of a public service officer who died on duty.

The applicant's name must be on the deed, and only one application is allowed per property. A reduction, if granted, shows on the bill received the following January. A surviving spouse can qualify between ages 59 and 65 under conditions the page lists. Call 355-8224 or stop in at Room 103 for forms.

How are Scioto County taxes handled when I sell the house?

Before accepting an offer, get a payoff from the Scioto County Treasurer for the parcel, delinquent balance included. The title company uses that figure to set aside tax money from your proceeds at closing. The deed then goes through the auditor, who endorses the conveyance, and on to the recorder.

A homestead reduction belongs to the qualifying owner. The auditor's page says changes in ownership must be reported, and the statement of value the buyer files under R.C. 319.202 asks the seller whether the property receives a tax reduction or an agricultural-use valuation. It also carries a notice to the buyer about eligibility for the reduction.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

What do monthly owner costs in Scioto County look like?

Federal data for 2020 to 2024 hint at what local owners carry. Median selected monthly owner costs run $1,277 for households with a mortgage and $493 for those without one, and a home's median value is $137,900. Property tax is one piece of those monthly costs, which is why a jump in assessed value is felt even by owners who have paid off their loans.

Seniors make up 20.6 percent of the population and veterans number 3,949, so many owners belong to groups the auditor's forms address. A county with 28,864 households and 2.40 people per household has plenty of filers to check against, so ask the auditor's office to confirm what your own parcel receives before you list the house.

More questions about Scioto County, OH Property Tax Guide

When are Scioto County property taxes due?

The statutory dates are December 31 and June 20. The county moved the second-half 2026 date to August 20, and that date has passed. Check the date printed on your own bill.

Who sends the property tax bill in Scioto County?

The treasurer, in Room 102 at 602 7th Street, Portsmouth, phone (740) 355-8272. The auditor sets values; the treasurer mails bills and takes payment.

How long do I have to dispute my Scioto County valuation?

Roughly until the end of March after the tax year; if first-half collection closes later, the window runs to that date instead. Send the complaint to the auditor, and the board of revision rules on it.

What penalty applies if I pay late?

R.C. 323.121 adds 10 percent to an unpaid first half, and another 10 percent to the unpaid current balance once the second-half date passes.

Does the homestead exemption move to the buyer of my house?

No. The break stays with the qualifying owner, and the auditor wants any change in ownership reported. A buyer has to qualify and apply separately.

Stark County by the numbers

Who bills and who values property tax in Stark County, Ohio?

Two elected offices split the work. The Stark County Auditor values every parcel and runs the exemption programs, and the Stark County Treasurer sends the bills and takes payment. Both are in Canton and both post weekday hours of 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., closed on government holidays.

Stark County property tax contacts, from the county's own pages
Office or deskWhat it handlesPhone
TreasurerBills, payments, delinquent taxes, foreclosure referrals330-451-7814
Auditor, appraisal departmentProperty values330-451-7085
Auditor, Board of RevisionValue complaints330-451-7998 or 330-451-7949
Auditor, homestead departmentHomestead and owner-occupancy reductions330-451-7323
Auditor, CAUVFarm use valuation330-451-7294
Auditor, real estate exemptionsExempt property330-451-7184
Auditor, destroyed propertyFire or storm damage to a building330-451-7949

The county seat is Canton, and the 374,853 residents counted in 2020 make Stark the eighth most populous county in Ohio. Its parcels fall into seventeen public school districts, from Canton City and Massillon City to Plain Local and Tuslaw Local, and the Treasurer's FAQ says most property tax dollars go to the schools in the owner's district. A tax rate table for each district is available in print at the Treasurer's office.

What are the Stark County tax payment dates and late rules?

Stark County bills in two halves. According to the Treasurer's FAQ, statements go out in January for a February deadline and again in June for July. The newspaper notice of the exact day runs about ten days ahead, and the day can shift: in 2026 the Treasurer's site blamed House Bill 186 for delays that moved the autopay letters from September to October.

  • The county gives no personal extensions. A bill turns late the morning after its stated due date.
  • Mailed payments count by the Postal Service postmark. A private meter stamp does not count, and a check dated after the deadline is treated as late.
  • Late current taxes pick up a ten percent penalty, per the FAQ, and balances left a full year gather interest.
  • A missing bill changes nothing. Download one from the Treasurer's website, ask for an emailed copy at 330-451-7814, or come to the counter.

The Treasurer's site also lists a monthly autopay program, which let enrolled owners spread a year's taxes over scheduled draws. Homeowners whose lender pays from escrow still get a courtesy copy each January. If the lender holds the wrong address after a refinance, the lender itself must ask the Treasurer in writing to fix it.

What does the Treasurer do about long-unpaid Stark County taxes?

Two tools are named in the FAQ. A tax lien certificate sale leaves title with the owner but lets the certificate buyer start a foreclosure if the lien stays open. A tax foreclosure, filed through the Prosecutor, ends in a public Sheriff's sale that does transfer title. The Treasurer's homepage announced a 2026 lien sale, saying that once letters go out only full payment in certified funds removes a parcel, along with a $200 lien fee.

The delinquent tax page lays out the court sequence. After the complaint reaches the Clerk of Courts, a certified-mail summons gives the owner 28 days to answer. An order of sale then moves to the Sheriff, and a newspaper runs the sale notice for three consecutive weeks. Redemption stays open until the court enters its confirmation, and it requires every tax, assessment, penalty, interest charge, fee and court cost, paid in certified funds.

A seller in this position has a known deadline: paying the full balance before the confirmation entry is how an owner redeems the parcel, whether the money comes from savings or from a sale.

Does Stark County offer a back-tax payment plan?

Yes, for delinquent balances only. The Treasurer sets these conditions on its delinquent tax page:

  • The signer must be the titled owner or a documented agent.
  • The delinquent balance has to be at least $1,000. A balance from $1,000 to $1,999 runs 12 months, and $2,000 or more runs 24 months.
  • At signing the owner pays 20 percent of the balance plus the current half.
  • Monthly installments fall on the 20th.
  • An owner who defaulted on an earlier contract cannot sign another.

The current year's bill must still be paid in full on time, and the page says the office cannot extend a due date or plan for current taxes. Any missed payment defaults the contract. Because a plan is a continuing obligation, a seller should ask the Treasurer for the payoff and settle it at closing.

How do I contest a Stark County valuation?

File a Board of Revision complaint with the Auditor by the March 31 deadline in ORC 5715.19, or by the close of first-half collection if that is later. Keep paying what you believe is due, since the Treasurer may accept the amount figured on your claimed value. The board has 180 days to rule. The state tax department says some counties run an informal review first, so ask the Stark appraisal department at 330-451-7085 whether that is available. Value is reset by a full reappraisal every six years and an update every three, so a parcel's schedule matters.

Which property tax breaks can a Stark County owner claim?

The Auditor's relief page lists homestead and owner occupancy, the Board of Revision complaint, CAUV for working farmland and exemption or special assessment matters. For tax year 2026 the Ohio Department of Taxation lists the senior and disabled homestead reduction at $29,700 of market value, with an application due December 31 of the year sought. A denial can be taken to the Board of Revision on form DTE 106B within 60 days.

House Bill 96 of 2025 also lets county commissioners add a local-option homestead exemption. The Homestead department at 330-451-7323 can say whether Stark County has adopted one.

What should a Stark County seller check on the tax side before closing?

Ask the Treasurer for the balance on each half, and have the title company confirm the payoff. The Auditor's transfer desk, reached at 330-451-7333, collects the conveyance fee and applies the stamp that the Recorder requires. Its page lists the rate per dollar of price and a per-parcel add-on, and it accepts only check or cash.

The Treasurer's site offers real estate search, prior-year search, the delinquent taxpayer list and a page for Sheriff sales. The delinquent list on the delinquent tax page was posted as of May 1, 2026. Stark County's settlement history helps explain the parcel map: the first permanent settlement came in 1805 at Canton, and the county, named for a Revolutionary War general, was created in 1808.

More questions about Stark County, OH Property Tax Guide

What is the penalty for paying Stark County property tax late?

Ten percent of the current tax, according to the Treasurer's FAQ. Interest also builds on balances that sit a full year. The county grants no individual extensions.

When do Stark County property tax bills go out?

January mailings serve the February payment, and June mailings serve July. Exact dates run in the Canton Repository shortly before each deadline and can move from year to year.

Can I set up a payment plan for Stark County back taxes?

Yes, but only for delinquent balances of $1,000 or more, and only for the titled owner who has not defaulted before. Expect 20 percent down plus the current half at signing, then payments on the 20th. Current-year tax is excluded.

Where do I file a Stark County property value complaint?

At the Stark County Auditor's office, which passes it to the Board of Revision. The board's lines are 330-451-7998 and 330-451-7949, and the state window closes at the end of March the following year.

Does a Stark County tax foreclosure take my house right away?

No. Several steps come first: a court complaint, a 28-day answer period, an order of sale and three weeks of advertising. The owner can still redeem before the court confirms the sale, using certified funds.

What we confirmed on official pages

Tax rate

Selling in Summit County?
We buy Summit County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

Summit County by the numbers

Which Summit County office do I call about real estate taxes?

Start with the Summit County Fiscal Office, which houses Auditor, Treasurer and Recorder divisions under a single elected Fiscal Officer. The Auditor division sets values and rates, the Treasurer division issues bills and takes money, and a Board of Revision hears value disputes.

The one-office setup comes from the county charter. Wikipedia notes that Summit and Cuyahoga are Ohio's only charter counties, and that Summit's fiscal officer does the work other counties spread across a separate auditor, treasurer and recorder. An executive and an eleven-member council stand in for the usual three commissioners.

Renovation of the Ohio Building at 175 S. Main St. in Akron pushed the Fiscal Office's divisions into temporary quarters, so phone first. The contact page carries these lines:

  • Main office: 1-888-388-5613
  • Treasurer: 330-643-2588
  • Real Estate and Appraisal, which handles homestead and assessments: 330-643-2710
  • Board of Revision: 330-926-2559 or bor@summitoh.net
  • Delinquent Tax Department: 330-643-2600

What kind of county is Summit for a house sale?

QuickFacts estimates about 538,000 residents in 2025 on 412.79 square miles of land, 0.4 percent under the 2020 base. Owner-occupied homes make up 67.5 percent of the stock, the median value of those homes is $208,700, and renters pay a median $1,026. Median household income is $71,622. Those medians cover the whole county, so any one street may differ.

Akron is the seat and largest city. The county dates to March 3, 1840, cut from Medina, Portage and Stark, and takes its name from the high point of the Ohio and Erie Canal. Cuyahoga Valley National Park fills much of the north. Barberton, Cuyahoga Falls, Fairlawn, Green, Hudson, Macedonia, Munroe Falls, New Franklin, Norton, Stow, Tallmadge and Twinsburg are the other cities, linked by I-76, I-77, I-271, I-480 and the Ohio Turnpike.

Seventy-four taxing authorities share the bill, per the Fiscal Office: the county, 5 county agencies, 26 school districts, 8 library districts, 14 cities, 8 villages, 9 townships, a water district, a fire district and a recreation district. The two leading digits of a parcel number identify your taxing district, and that district decides the rate.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Summit County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What goes into a Summit County tax bill?

Ohio taxes 35 percent of appraised value. The rate stacks up levies that local voters approved. The Fiscal Officer states on the tax rates page that the office has no power to raise or lower taxes, and the page links three years of effective rate summaries. It sorts levies into five kinds:

  • Additional: new money for a taxing body, so bills rise.
  • Renewal: the same yield as an expiring levy.
  • Replacement: swaps in current values for a levy built on old ones, so bills move with the market.
  • Emergency: schools only, a fixed yearly sum over a stated span.
  • Bond: covers principal and interest on a permanent improvement.

The bill explanation lists the summary of charges: reduction factor, non-business credit, owner-occupancy credit, homestead reduction, current net taxes and current assessments. A bill covers the year before, because Ohio collects one year in arrears. Akron residents with an assessment question call 330-375-2484, and everyone else calls 330-643-2645.

How late can I pay, and what does a miss cost?

Dates print on the bill. The Fiscal Office FAQ says there is no grace period and that never receiving a bill is no defense. A missed first half draws a 10 percent penalty. Miss the second half too and the full unpaid current balance, first-half amount included, takes another 10 percent. Per R.C. 323.121(C), paying everything within ten days after a deadline halves that penalty.

Payment channels named in the FAQ:

  • A counter visit to the Treasurer division, checks payable to the Fiscal Officer or Fiscal Office.
  • Mail with a U.S. postmark on or before the deadline. Private meter stamps are rejected.
  • A bank listed on your bill, available only while a collection is open.
  • Phone or web through Official Payments Corporation, which charges 1 percent on debit (minimum $3.95), 2.75 percent on credit (minimum $3.95) or $1.00 per electronic check, per the online payments page.
  • Cash at a MoneyGram location, plus a service fee.

Summit's charter lets it run a prepayment plan, the Real Estate Discount program. Owners with no delinquency sign up between July 1 and October 31 for a first half, or between January 1 and March 31 for a second half, pay on five of six coupons and earn credit on the early money. Missing the last coupon forfeits the credit.

What is the route for disputing a Summit County valuation?

Use the Board of Revision, whose window runs from the first of January through the end of March. It rules on value alone and never on the tax amount, and the owner has to prove the claim with paperwork.

Summit County Board of Revision at a glance, per the Fiscal Office complaint page
ItemDetail
WindowJanuary 1 to March 31
DeliveryMail postmarked by the deadline, a counter visit, or Smartfile online
SeatsFiscal Officer, County Executive, Clerk of Courts, or designees
ProofHanded in, mailed, or uploaded with an online filing
Legal weightFiling starts a legal proceeding

Values are redone every six years, with an update in year three, by comparing a parcel with neighborhood sales. Permits tip off the office to new building. Rewiring, replumbing, framing or foundation work can raise value, while a new roof or routine remodeling does not.

With a complaint pending, R.C. 5715.19 allows you to tender tax computed on your claimed value, with interest on any shortfall if the final number lands higher. Evidence withheld from the board can be excluded on appeal. For storm, fire, flood or demolition damage, file DTE Form 26 by December 31 (damage in the year's first nine months) or by January 31 (last three months).

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Summit County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Which tax reductions can a Summit County seller or heir use?

The homestead exemption removes the first $29,000 of appraised value on a single-family home from tax, and the office puts average savings at $535 yearly. It covers owners 65 by December 31, the permanently and totally disabled, veterans rated 100 percent for service-connected disability, and spouses of first responders who died on duty. Veterans see $58,000 exempted. The 2026 income ceiling for age and disability claims is $41,000, using the owner's and spouse's Ohio adjusted gross income.

The owner-occupancy reduction needs you to own and live in the home on January 1, with the application in by December 31. Rentals are out. It ends when the property transfers, so an incoming owner-occupant files again.

At transfer, R.C. 319.202 has the buyer's conveyance statement confirm that the seller was asked about these reductions. If the house gets one, a sworn note estimating the amount travels with it. Your title company will request the answer.

What can I do about back taxes on a Summit County house?

The Delinquent Tax Payment Plan, started in 1987, takes owners who missed a half and sets monthly installments. The old balance freezes in a special account with no added interest, leftover interest is abated at completion, and new bills must be paid on time.

The office sells tax certificate liens each late October. Paying in full or entering a plan keeps a lien off that sale. If you would rather sell, ask the title company to request a payoff figure from the Treasurer division and settle it at closing.

More questions about Summit County, OH Property Tax Guide

What is the late fee on Summit County property tax?

It is 10 percent of the unpaid half. Full payment within ten days after the deadline gets half of that penalty waived under state law.

Can I use the Real Estate Discount program while I owe back taxes?

No. Taxes must be current to enroll. Owners who are behind should ask about the Delinquent Tax Payment Plan.

How soon must I report fire or storm damage to the Fiscal Office?

File DTE Form 26 by December 31 for damage from January through September, or by January 31 of the following year for October through December damage. Send it to appraisedvalue@summitoh.net or mail it in.

Where is my parcel number?

The Fiscal Office property search finds it from a name, address or the number itself. Its first two digits name the taxing district.

Does a postmark on the due date count?

A Postal Service postmark on the due date counts, while a private meter mark does not. Under state law the earliest postmark on the envelope sets the payment date.

What we could not confirm

  • Trumbull recorder e-recording
  • Trumbull delinquent tax/foreclosure facts

Trumbull County by the numbers

Which Trumbull County office does what with my tax bill?

Two courthouse-square offices split the work from the second floor of the Administration Building at 160 High Street NW in Warren. The Auditor sets values, takes homestead applications and receives Board of Revision complaints. The Treasurer prints the bills and collects the money.

  • Auditor: 330-675-2420, or 330-675-2895 for questions about a specific valuation.
  • Treasurer: 330-675-2436, with no lunchtime closing, per its FAQ.
  • Board of Revision filings by email: BOR@co.trumbull.oh.us.

Rate cards for each taxing district, back to 2010, are linked from the Treasurer's tax information page. Bills, payment history and values live in the Auditor's online property search, except manufactured homes, which are not listed there and need a call to the Treasurer.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Trumbull County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What sets Trumbull County apart for a house seller?

Trumbull fills the far northeast corner of Ohio with a square outline about 25 miles across, a shape Wikipedia says no other Ohio county shares. Established in 1800, it once held the entire Connecticut Western Reserve, and Warren began as that territory's capital. Today Warren is the seat. Cortland, Girard, Hubbard and Niles are the other cities, a slice of Youngstown extends in from the south, and I-80, US 62, US 422 and State Route 11 carry the traffic.

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts table estimates 198,972 people for 2025, a 1.5 percent slide since 2020, in 94,514 housing units. Owners hold 71.3 percent of occupied homes. The middle owner-occupied home is valued at $141,800 for 2020 to 2024, the median rent is $797 and median household income is $56,435. Nearly a quarter of residents, 24.3 percent, are 65 or older, so the age-based homestead exemption touches many sellers. Permit activity is light, with 112 building permits in 2025.

When does Trumbull County collect, and where do I pay?

Collections come twice a year, usually around March and August, with the exact days printed on each bill. For 2025 taxes payable in 2026 the Treasurer posted March 6 and August 31, 2026, and manufactured homes ran March 2 and August 21, 2026. Bills tend to go out by the end of January and again by the end of June. Early payment earns no discount.

Payment choices on the Treasurer's pages:

  • Mail a check or money order to the Treasurer, 160 High Street NW, Floor 2A, Warren, OH 44481. The postmark date is honored.
  • Drop it in the box on Harmon Avenue beside the building's side steps, open around the clock for checks and money orders.
  • Go online through the Auditor's property search and its Tax tab, using an e-check, debit card or credit card.
  • Pay at the counter with cash, check, card or money order.

A processing company charges $1.00 per e-check and 2.5 percent of the total on cards, and the county gets none of it. A returned check costs $15.00. One check may cover several parcels if the parcel numbers are on the memo line. Allow 7 to 10 days after a collection closes for payments to post.

Owners with nothing past due can enroll in the Tax Installment Payment Plan, which prepays through monthly coupons. Ask the Treasurer for a TIP clerk.

How does the Trumbull County Auditor decide what my house is worth?

The Auditor describes a mass appraisal for roughly 144,000 parcels: one method, common data, statistical testing. Inputs include field verification, aerial photos, owner-sent settlement statements or appraisals, auction results and listing-service data. Staff generally cannot enter your home, which is a main reason a single bank appraisal can differ. The county compares three years of sales, and the work takes about two and a half years.

The assessed share is 35 percent of market value. The Auditor's guide to the 2023 reappraisal says Ohio requires a countywide update every three years and that rates then adjust so voted levies raise the same money as before. Only inside millage, 10 mills at most, floats with value. Special assessments for ditches, paving, curbs, sewer and water lines, lighting and trash removal share the bill but are separate from tax.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Trumbull County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How do I challenge a Trumbull County valuation?

Go through the Board of Revision, which weighs value and never the tax dollars. State law, R.C. 5715.19, closes the window on March 31 or when first-half collection ends, whichever is later. The person complaining has to prove the case.

Trumbull County Board of Revision, from the Auditor's board page
StageWhat happens
MembersAuditor, Treasurer and Commissioners, each free to send a stand-in
FormsDTE 1, 1M or 2 for value; DTE 106B for homestead or owner-occupancy disputes
DeliveryEmail, mail, fax or in person; a handwritten form needs a notary, an electronic one does not
First lookSome files draw a proposed value that you can take or turn down
Hearing noticeAt least 10 days before, in person, by phone or on Webex
EvidenceBest sent with the complaint, and no later than 7 days ahead
Next level30 days from the decision letter to the Board of Tax Appeals or Common Pleas

The board lists an independent appraisal, photos, repair estimates, and a settlement statement with the purchase agreement as common evidence. A school board can counter-file within 30 days. The Auditor warns that taxes stay due during a complaint and that paying in full prevents penalty trouble, with any reduction returned as a credit or refund.

Which Trumbull County reductions can help a seller or heir?

The Auditor's homestead page explains three:

  • Homestead exemption: up to $29,000 off market value. Owners must be 65 or older, or permanently and totally disabled, or a surviving spouse who was 59 or older when a recipient died. The income cap is $41,000 for 2026 taxes payable in 2027, and $40,000 for a late application on 2025 taxes payable in 2026, using Ohio adjusted gross income for owner and spouse.
  • Disabled veteran exemption: up to $58,000 for veterans rated 100 percent permanently disabled from service, with no income cap.
  • Owner-occupancy reduction: close to 2.5 percent off the bill while the owner lives there, with no filing deadline. It covers the home and one acre.

Appeal a denial on form DTE 106B within 60 days of the notice. Manufactured home owners have until January 31 of the next year. Separately, form DTE 23A asks for remission of a late-payment penalty. The taxpayer files it with the Treasurer, and the board reviews it when the Auditor cannot grant it.

Who owes the tax when a Trumbull County house changes hands?

The Treasurer's FAQ says the owner of record when a bill comes due is responsible, and each bill carries the deeded owner as of the start of the tax year. Sellers and buyers should read their purchase agreement for who reimburses whom. The Treasurer does not keep that agreement, so a title or mortgage company is the place to ask.

At the Auditor's conveyance desk, a transfer costs $4.00 per thousand of value plus $0.50 per parcel, and an exempt transfer costs only the parcel charge. A deed travels to the Tax Map office, then the Auditor, then the Recorder, with a clear copy of the last deed of record. By mail, add a stamped return envelope and a check to the Trumbull County Auditors Office.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

What happens to unpaid taxes on a Trumbull County house?

Tax foreclosure sales are held in person every other Thursday at 1:30 p.m. in the Commissioners' hearing room, under rules effective May 7, 2026. Bidding starts at a minimum and rises by $100. The top bidder leaves $3,000 in certified funds and owes the balance 30 days after the sale is confirmed. The owner can redeem until the judge signs that confirmation. Bank mortgage foreclosures have moved to an online site under House Bill 390.

The Trumbull County Land Bank, formed in late 2010 through the Treasurer's office, acquires vacant, tax-delinquent parcels and markets them for reuse, working with Trumbull Neighborhood Partnership. If you would rather sell before things reach that point, ask the title company to request a payoff amount from the Treasurer.

More questions about Trumbull County, OH Property Tax Guide

Does Trumbull County count the postmark on a mailed payment?

Yes. The Treasurer honors the postmark date on mailed payments, though posting can take 7 to 10 days after a collection closes.

Can I get a discount for paying the whole Trumbull County bill early?

No. The Treasurer's FAQ says early full payment earns nothing. Owners who are current can use the monthly coupon plan instead.

Who pays the tax if I sell in the middle of the year?

The owner of record when the bill is due owes it. Your purchase agreement sets who reimburses whom, so read it or ask the title company.

What if the Auditor denies my homestead exemption?

File form DTE 106B with the Board of Revision within 60 days of the denial notice. Manufactured home owners have until January 31 of the following year.

Is there a fee for paying by card?

Yes, 2.5 percent of the total, paid to the processing company. E-checks cost $1.00. Cash, checks and money orders avoid the fee.

Tax rate

Selling in Union County?
We buy Union County houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Union County by the numbers

Which Union County offices handle property tax?

Everything tax-related sits in one place: the County Office Building at 233 West Sixth Street, Marysville, Ohio 43040. Three of them matter to a seller.

  • Auditor. Sets values, keeps the tax credits, runs the Board of Revision complaint process and stamps deeds. Phone 937-645-3003.
  • Treasurer. Sends bills and collects payment; a drop box sits at the rear entrance. Phone 937-645-3035, open weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., closed on federal holidays.
  • Recorder. Files the deed and any mortgage release after the auditor's stamp. Phone 937-645-3032.

The auditor's page puts the county at about 32,800 property records, and the treasurer's page describes more than 30,000 parcels. By the treasurer's account, roughly 70 percent of what the office collects goes to local schools.

How does Union County calculate a property tax bill?

Each parcel gets a market value from the auditor, and the treasurer's FAQ puts assessed value at 35 percent of it. The assessed value is multiplied by the total tax rate for the parcel's district, then reduced by credits.

  • Residential and agricultural property gets a 10 percent credit on the net tax for levies passed before November 2013.
  • A home the owner lives in earns an extra 2 1/2 percent credit on the house and up to an acre, once the owner files form DTE 105C.
  • Levies passed after November 2013 that raise funding do not carry the rollbacks.
  • The Homestead Exemption is open to owners who are 65 or older or permanently disabled, subject to an income test in place since 2014.

Ohio caps unvoted taxation at ten mills per thousand dollars of assessed value, and any levy beyond that needs a vote. The county's tax rate page lists rates by district and levy, and the DTE 515 report gives the composite reduction factors. To see your rate, find the parcel on the auditor's website and follow the “Where your taxes go” link. The first two digits of the parcel number identify the tax district.

Where a house sits matters for schools. The auditor's GIS notes that when a district line crosses a house, the school district where the master bedroom is located governs the whole house.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Union County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What are the Union County due dates and penalties?

Bills are mailed in January and June, and Ohio collects a year behind. A bill that arrives in 2026 covers tax year 2025. The county sets each year's dates, and the treasurer's FAQ says the first half usually falls in mid-February and the second half in mid-July or August. The county's 2026 schedule is below.

Union County treasurer calendar for 2025 taxes payable in 2026
DateWhat happened or applies
February 18, 2026First half due
February 19 and 28, 20265 percent, then 10 percent penalty added to unpaid first half
August 12, 2026Second half due
August 13 and 22, 20265 percent, then 10 percent penalty added to unpaid 2025 tax
September 1, 20264.67 percent interest on unpaid prior years' delinquency
December 1, 20262.33 percent interest on the total unpaid balance

Source: Union County Treasurer payment information.

The postal cancellation date controls for mailed checks; a stamp from a private postage meter does not count. The county also says a missing bill never excuses a late payment. Before the second half came due in 2026, the treasurer advised paying only the first half, because House Bill 186 required rates to be recalculated for the second half. The treasurer said overpayments would be credited or refunded.

How do you pay a Union County tax bill, or spread it out?

Checks go to the Union County Treasurer at the Sixth Street address, by mail, in person or in the back drop box. The county takes cards and e-checks online, and the treasurer's FAQ says a processing fee goes to the payment vendor rather than the county. In 2026 the treasurer also accepted payments at a Richwood bank on set days before each due date, so check the payment information page for any such location.

Two programs help with budgeting:

  • Real Estate Tax Escrow Program. Prepay by the month, and the treasurer applies the funds as each half comes due.
  • Delinquent payment plan. A written contract with the treasurer lets you pay back taxes in installments while keeping current tax paid. Penalty and interest are held in escrow and removed once the contract is paid off, and added back if you default.

Unpaid bills draw a delinquent notice in late September or early October, and the owner's name is printed in the paper's delinquent list. When tax is still owed the following November, the file goes to the county prosecutor to begin foreclosure.

How do you challenge a Union County valuation?

The auditor receives each complaint and passes it to the Board of Revision. State law sets the cutoff in Ohio Revised Code 5715.19: March 31, or the day first-half collection closes if that is later.

  • File a notarized DTE Form 1 by email, fax or mail to the Auditor's Office, Attn: Board of Revision, at the Sixth Street address.
  • Contest only the current tax year. The board does not look back.
  • Attach a closing statement, purchase contract, escrow statement and deed if you bought or sold recently.
  • Hearing dates follow the order in which complaints are received.
  • A property held by a business or trust should use an attorney. An individual does not need one.

If the change you seek tops $50,000 in market value (or $17,500 assessed), the school board is notified. Board decisions are held for 30 days, and a refund or credit follows about sixty days after that. A disappointed owner has 30 days from the decision letter to appeal, either to the Ohio Board of Tax Appeals on DTE Form 4 or to the Court of Common Pleas. In many cases a decision holds until the next triennial update. The auditor reports the last full reappraisal in 2019, with updates every third year after.

What tax relief programs does Union County offer?

Besides the rollbacks above, the auditor administers two programs that a buyer or seller may ask about.

  • Homestead Exemption. The county page lists age 65 or older, permanent disability, or a surviving spouse aged 59 to 64 of a person already receiving the exemption. The applicant must own the house and live in it, and June's first Monday is the filing cutoff. Disabled veterans use form DTE 105I. Ask the auditor for the current income cap.
  • Current Agricultural Use Value (CAUV). Land of at least ten acres worked commercially for three years can be taxed on what it earns as farmland. A parcel under ten acres needs $2,500 average yearly gross income. Applications are timed to the calendar: they count only if the auditor's office has them in hand after the January date and before the March one, regardless of postmark. Pulling out of the program triggers a charge equal to the previous three years of tax savings.

When a property sells, section 319.202 asks the grantee to affirm whether the seller said the property carried a rollback or CAUV status. A seller with CAUV land should talk to the auditor before closing about the recoupment charge.

How does property tax work at a Union County closing?

The settlement statement normally prorates the tax, which ends the seller's responsibility for later bills. The treasurer's FAQ tells a seller who still receives a bill to hand it to the new owner or phone the office, so a corrected bill can go out. Look at the settlement statement, since a bill for the prior year can come due after you have moved.

The county is growing quickly. In Census Bureau figures, the county reached an estimated 73,446 residents in 2025, a 17.0 percent rise on the 2020 base. The typical owned home is valued at $344,900, and 968 building permits were issued in 2025. Several school systems share the county: Marysville Exempted Village, Fairbanks, North Union and Triad, along with parts of Jonathan Alder, Buckeye Valley, Elgin, Benjamin Logan and Dublin City.

Ask the title company to check for delinquent tax, and ask the treasurer for the rate sheet covering your district.

More questions about Union County, OH Property Tax Guide

What are the Union County due dates and penalties?

Mid-February is typical for the first half, with the second half falling between mid-July and August. The treasurer announces exact dates yearly; for tax year 2025 they were February 18 and August 12, 2026.

What penalty applies to a late Union County tax payment?

Under the 2026 schedule, a 5 percent penalty hit the day after each due date and rose to 10 percent ten days later. Interest on older delinquent tax followed on September 1, with another charge on December 1.

How do I appeal my Union County property value?

The complaint must be notarized. Email, fax or post it to the Auditor's Office in Marysville, Attn: Board of Revision, between January 1 and March 31 following the tax year.

Can I pay my Union County taxes monthly?

Yes. The Real Estate Tax Escrow Program lets you prepay on a monthly basis, and the treasurer applies the funds when each half comes due. Contact the treasurer's office to enroll.

Who pays the property tax when a Union County home sells?

The settlement statement divides the year's tax by date. Later bills belong to the buyer. If one still lands in the former owner's mailbox, hand it over or ask the treasurer to reissue it.

Which Warren County offices deal with property tax?

Two elected offices split the work. The Warren County Auditor values property and administers credits, and the Warren County Treasurer sends the bills and takes payment. The auditor's office is at 406 Justice Drive in Lebanon, and its real estate department answers at 513-695-1235.

The auditor's real estate page says the office maintains records on about 91,400 parcels, covering ownership, legal description, property address, building description, appraised value and the transfer history that feeds the tax list. The treasurer posts rate sheets for every year from 2004 through 2025, so a seller can look up how a parcel's levies have moved.

Complaints about value go to the Board of Revision, a panel of three that seats the auditor, the treasurer and the commissioners' president.

How does Warren County value a house for tax?

Each parcel is appraised at estimated fair market value and taxed at 35 percent of it, which is how the auditor's appraisal page describes Ohio's common level of assessment. Every parcel gets a site visit in a general reappraisal at least once every six years, and a triennial update adjusts values in the third year between those cycles, usually by percentage changes drawn from local sales.

New construction and changes in use are valued every year. The tax lien date is January 1, so ownership and use on that day fix the bill payable the following year.

The auditor's own FAQ says most increases follow the state-required reappraisal, and that without new construction or new levies, bills tend to stay close to the same level between updates. A school levy passed by voters in a district raises bills for the parcels inside it, which is why two similar homes in different school districts can pay different amounts. Warren County has ten school districts, from Carlisle and Clinton-Massie to Kings, Lebanon, Mason and Springboro, plus a career center.

When are Warren County property taxes due?

Ohio real estate tax is billed in two halves. For tax year 2025 the treasurer's page printed February 25, 2026 for the first half and August 12, 2026 for the second. The August date was an extension the Tax Commissioner approved after House Bill 186's inflation cap credit delayed the second-half bills, and the treasurer asked owners to wait for the bill rather than send an estimate.

Taxes can be paid through the myWarrenCountyOhio portal, by calling 513-496-2931, or in person weekdays between 7:30 am and 4:30 pm. Forms posted on the treasurer's page:

  • Military Extension Application.

Late charges come from Revised Code 323.121: an unpaid half draws a ten percent penalty, cut in half when the whole amount arrives within ten days of the deadline. Delinquent balances also collect interest at the rate set under section 5703.47.

How do you appeal a Warren County property value?

If you believe the auditor's value is too high, form DTE 1 is the tool, and the auditor accepts it from January 1 through March 31 of the next tax year. A notary must witness the signature of the owner or the owner's attorney.

What the board decides is market value for land and buildings together, never the tax dollars or rates. Because the owner carries the burden of proof, a weak case can leave the value alone or push it up. The board sends notice at least ten days before the recorded hearing and later mails or emails a decision letter to each party.

  • The auditor's FAQ names three good kinds of evidence: a recent sale for less than the county's value, a recent fee appraisal, and proof of damage or defects that hurt the home's worth.
  • The board may also request purchase or lease agreements, closing statements, construction cost records, rent rolls and income and expense statements.
  • Get supporting papers to the board before the hearing date.

What tax breaks does Warren County offer homeowners?

The homestead page capped income for the 2026 tax year at $41,000 of 2025 Ohio adjusted gross income. Owners who miss the cutoff can reapply the next year, when the state may raise it. A disability claim needs Certificate of Disability form DTE 105E or another accepted certification.

Two other reductions are worth knowing. Damaged or destroyed buildings can earn a value deduction on form DTE 26, filed by December 31 for damage in the first nine months of a year or by January 31 for damage in the last three, with the share granted set by the quarter: 100 percent for January to March, 75 for April to June, 50 for July to September and 25 for October to December. Farmland in the CAUV program is valued on expected farm income, open to farms over 10 acres in commercial use for three years and to smaller ones grossing at least $2,500 a year, with a $25 first-time filing fee and a payback of up to three years of savings if the use changes.

What changes on the tax side when a Warren County home sells?

The auditor transfers the deed on the tax list before the recorder sees it. The auditor's transfer page lists three charges: a conveyance fee, a county transfer tax and a per-parcel transfer fee, all due before the deed goes on to the recorder.

The state's statement of value, set out in section 319.202, asks whether the home's taxes are reduced under the homestead or owner-occupied credit statute, and whether the land carried CAUV value. A yes means a sworn paper estimating the reduction or the recoupment, signed by buyer and seller. The statement also reminds the buyer to tell the auditor if the home later stops qualifying for the reduction.

One more Ohio rule applies to landlords: when the house is residential rental property, the auditor's endorsement on the deed tells the new owner to file rental registration information.

What should a Warren County seller with back taxes do?

Before listing, ask the treasurer for a written payoff covering penalties and interest. The title company will want it for the closing statement. The Application for Remission of Late Payment Penalties on the treasurer's page is the way to ask for relief.

The county also runs forfeited land sales, and the auditor's home page announced one for November 9, 2026. Ask either office how a delinquent parcel moves toward that kind of sale, and settle the balance early.

Who sends the property tax bill in Warren County, Ohio?

The Warren County Treasurer does. The auditor sets the value, and the treasurer bills, collects and posts rate sheets. Payment options include myWarrenCountyOhio, and phone at 513-496-2931.

What percent of market value does Warren County tax?

Thirty-five percent of appraised value is the taxable value, as the auditor's appraisal page explains. The auditor reappraises every parcel at least once in six years and updates values in the third year between.

What is the deadline to challenge a Warren County valuation?

March 31 closes the window. A DTE 1 complaint can go to the auditor starting January 1 of the following tax year, and the signature has to be notarized.

What income limit applies to the Warren County homestead exemption?

For the 2026 tax year the auditor's page lists $41,000 of 2025 Ohio adjusted gross income. To qualify you must be 65, permanently disabled, or a surviving spouse of a past participant who is at least 59. Applications must be at the auditor by December 31.

Can I get Warren County late-payment penalties removed?

You can apply. The treasurer's page posts an Application for Remission of Late Payment Penalties and a Military Extension Application. Under Ohio law, paying the full amount within ten days of the due date also cuts the penalty in half.

Wayne County by the numbers

What should a seller know about Wayne County, Ohio, before reading a tax bill?

Wooster anchors Wayne County in the northeast quarter of Ohio. Legislators described the county in 1808, the first officials began work in January 1812, and the name honors General Anthony Wayne. Medina and Summit counties lie north, Stark east, Holmes south, Ashland west.

About 555 square miles of land make up the county, which on its own forms the Wooster micropolitan area. Students attend schools feeding Wooster, Orrville, Rittman, Smithville, Dalton, Chippewa, Northwestern, Norwayne, Triway and Waynedale high schools, and the College of Wooster sits in the seat. Tax matters run through 428 West Liberty Street, where the Auditor, the Treasurer and the Board of Revision share an address.

How do Wayne County owners and housing costs line up in the Census data?

Ownership runs high here. The Census Bureau reports 116,758 residents as of July 2025 and 44,365 households, with 76.6 percent of homes lived in by their owners over 2020 to 2024.

The Auditor's home page counts 59,000 parcels, so the Treasurer mails a very large number of bills twice a year.

How is a Wayne County tax bill put together?

According to the Auditor, each parcel is taxed on 35 percent of market value. Multiply that taxable figure by the rate for your district, then subtract the reduction factor that keeps voted levies at the revenue voters approved.

  • A rollback credit from 1971 applies to most residential parcels.
  • A separate credit helps owner-occupied homes, covering the dwelling and up to one acre of home site.
  • County millage pays for the general fund, children services, the County Care Center, Medway Drug Enforcement and the board of developmental disabilities.
  • Libraries, fire districts and Wayne Holmes Mental Health fall under "Other" on the distribution panel, next to township, city and school levies.

Unvoted millage stops at 10 mills under Ohio law. A chart of districts and rates sits on the Treasurer's tax information page.

What are the Wayne County installment dates and late charges?

Bills arrive in two installments. January or February brings the first, June or July the second, and each bill prints its own due date. The Treasurer's site listed these 2026 dates.

Past the due date, the Treasurer's FAQ says, a 10 percent penalty is added, and the auditor gives back half if the balance is cleared inside 10 days. Cards and mobile wallets work through Autoagent for a 2.35 percent fee with a $2.00 floor. The e-check fee is $0.50, and a bounced check costs $15.00. Postmarks count on mailed payments, though the Treasurer cautions that a postmark can trail the day you mailed, and the September delinquent cycle takes none.

Nothing in the mail by July 1 means a call to 330-287-5450. State law at R.C. 323.13 treats a missing bill as no excuse.

What steps does a Wayne County owner follow to dispute a value?

Disputes go to the Board of Revision through the Auditor. The window opens January 1 and closes March 31, subject to the later-date rule in R.C. 5715.19. For tax year 2026 the Auditor posts January 1, 2027 to March 31, 2027.

  • Sign the complaint before a notary. Auditor staff will usually notarize it at the counter.
  • Postmark mail by March 31. Send email or fax before 11:59 pm that night.
  • Expect one complaint per three-year cycle, with exceptions for an arm's length sale, casualty loss, major improvement or a 15 percent occupancy swing.
  • Keep paying the first half bill. The second half bill waits until the Board rules, then reflects the difference.

The county's 2026 reappraisal has an informal stage that the Auditor's home page says has closed, with formal filings opening January 1, 2027. Call the Board of Revision at 330-287-5433.

Which relief programs does the Wayne County Auditor run?

Three programs sit with the Auditor: the homestead exemption, the owner-occupied credit and current agricultural use value. The forms library lists DTE 105A (homestead application), 105B (continuing application), 105C (owner-occupancy credit), 105E (disability certificate) and 105I (disabled veterans and surviving spouses).

Exemption applications for churches, schools, nonprofits and public land are filed there too. Age and income limits shift between tax years, so call the real estate division at 330-287-5430 for the numbers that apply to you before counting on a credit.

What happens at the Auditor's counter when a Wayne County house sells?

The deed makes a short trip inside one building: Map Office, then Auditor, then Recorder. Four dollars per thousand of price is the conveyance rate the Auditor prints, with 50 cents per parcel on top, and the price is rounded up to the next $100.

  • The Auditor's page lists recording at $34.00 for two pages and $8.00 per extra page.
  • A grantee's value statement under R.C. 319.202 must precede the Auditor's endorsement.
  • Online tools include a conveyance calculator, a tax estimator and a levy estimator.

Settle tax proration in the contract, and get a payoff from the Treasurer for any parcel carrying a balance. The delinquent list on the Treasurer's site shows parcels with unpaid years.

How does the 2026 Wayne County reappraisal reach a seller's value?

Ohio requires the Auditor to run a countywide reappraisal every six years. Once a final abstract of values is approved by the state, new tax rates for the next tax year follow from those values, the levies voters passed and the 10 mills receivable by the county. If values climb, the state applies reduction factors so a levy cannot raise more than the amount first voted.

Wayne County's 2026 reappraisal opens the three-year cycle that the one-complaint rule above refers to. The Auditor's home page describes how to find a new proposed value, what to do next, and the dates for the informal and formal stages. Look up your parcel on the Auditor's site before you set an asking price.

Which Wayne County properties are exempt or taxed differently?

Land leased out for profit, or vacant with no planned use, does not qualify.

  • Community Reinvestment Area abatements are available only where a city, village or county has had an area approved by the state development agency.
  • Tax increment financing diverts part of the tax on added value to the municipality or to a city and school combination.
  • Manufactured homes are billed on a separate duplicate. The Treasurer's page says the tax base is 40 percent of depreciated value under the older rule, and that a 1998 law moved new assessments toward market value.

The Treasurer's calendar shows February 26 and July 30, 2026 as the final days, with February 2 and July 13 for bank payments. Every bill prints its own deadline.

From January 1 through March 31. The Auditor's page gives January 1, 2027 to March 31, 2027 for tax year 2026, and mailed complaints need a March 31 postmark.

The Auditor's page prints four dollars per $1,000 of price plus $0.50 per parcel, with price rounded up to the next $100. The Auditor's calculator does the arithmetic.

Does the Wayne County Treasurer accept cards?

Yes, including Apple Pay, Google Pay and Samsung Pay, online, at 1-844-615-1900 or at the office. Expect a 2.35 percent charge with a $2.00 floor, or $0.50 by e-check.

Where do I file a deed after closing in Wayne County?

With the Recorder on the first floor of 428 West Liberty Street in Wooster, 330-287-5460, once the Auditor has endorsed it. Deeds, mortgages, liens and plats are filed there.

What does a seller need to know about Wood County, Ohio, geography and taxing districts?

The Maumee River bends along the northwest side of Wood County, whose 617 square miles of land are hemmed in by Lucas, Ottawa, Sandusky, Seneca, Hancock, Putnam and Henry counties. Toledo's metropolitan area includes it. The county dates to 1820. Perrysburg held the courthouse first, and the seat shifted to Bowling Green in 1870.

City governments exist in Bowling Green, Northwood, Perrysburg and Rossford, and a sliver of Fostoria reaches in. Fifteen school districts draw on county land: Anthony Wayne, Bowling Green City, Eastwood, Elmwood, Fostoria City, Gibsonburg, Lake, Lakota, McComb, North Baltimore, Northwood, Otsego, Patrick Henry, Perrysburg and Rossford. The Auditor sets values and the Treasurer sends bills, with both offices at the Bowling Green courthouse square. Ground for that courthouse was broken November 28, 1893, once citizens chose to move the seat from Perrysburg.

What does QuickFacts report on Wood County homes and renters?

The July 2025 estimate is 134,176 residents, up 1.5 percent on the 2020 base, in 54,257 households. Owners hold 64.4 percent of the homes for 2020 to 2024, so a little over a third of households rent. The survey also counts 5,955 veterans, the population behind the Auditor's disabled veteran program.

What did the 2026 triennial update do to Wood County home values?

Countywide, residential values went up 19 percent on average, per the Auditor's press release. Ohio schedules a full reappraisal every sixth year and an update midway. Wood County reappraised in 2023, which put 2026 on the calendar for a neighborhood-level adjustment.

The new values belong to tax year 2026, collected in February and July 2027, and carry a January 1, 2026 lien date. Sales from the prior three years drive the statistics, and only arm's length sales count. One parcel can land above or below that average depending on location and condition.

Bills should not follow values one for one. According to the Auditor, House Bill 920 trims voted outside millage as values rise, House Bill 186 creates an inflation cap credit for school districts, and House Bill 335 does the same for inside millage, the unvoted portion held to 10 mills. A renewal levy keeps its current millage, a renewal with an increase adds to it, and an additional levy is a brand new tax.

What are the Wood County installment months, penalties and payment methods?

Real estate and manufactured home taxes come due in February and July, on dates the Treasurer announces each year. Roughly 80 taxing districts apply separate rates. Per the Treasurer's information page, paying late costs 5 percent during the first 10 days and 10 percent after that.

Where does a Wood County owner go to contest a value?

A formal complaint is filed with the Auditor for the Board of Revision, and the Auditor's real estate page puts the window at January 1 through March 31. For the 2026 values the update FAQ names March 31, 2027. Many owners try an informal review first.

  • Evidence for an informal review: a recent appraisal (under two years), three or more comparable sales from 2023 to 2025, or a sales listing.
  • The FAQ says a disputed amount above $50,000 requires a Board of Revision filing.
  • Comparable sales can be pulled with the Sales List, Sales Search or Comp Search tools, and the Comp Search is called the most useful.
  • R.C. 5715.19 caps owners at one complaint per interim period, with exceptions for a sale, casualty, major improvement or occupancy change after the lien date.

The real estate office, on the county office building's second floor, answers at 419-354-9173.

Which Wood County programs lower the tax on a home or farm?

The Auditor's tax reduction page lists these programs.

  • Homestead exemption, for owners 65 or older or permanently and totally disabled. The page prints a modified adjusted gross income ceiling of $40,000 for late applicants on tax year 2025 and $41,000 for new applicants on tax year 2026, and the house must be the primary residence.
  • Disabled veteran homestead exemption, for qualified veterans or surviving spouses.
  • Owner occupied reduction, by application, for the home an owner lives in.
  • Agricultural use valuation, for 10 or more acres in farming, with a $25.00 fee on new applications and a penalty if the land is sold, drops under 10 acres or stops being farmed.

A free agricultural district application protects farmland from certain water and sewer assessments. Homestead questions go to 419-354-9167, and agricultural programs to 419-354-9174.

What does a Wood County seller pay when the deed transfers?

Wood County's Auditor charges $3.00 per $1,000 of price on a deed, with the price bumped up to the nearest hundred, and adds $0.50 per parcel as a transfer fee. Exempt deeds use form DTE 100(EX).

R.C. 319.202 has the grantee file a value statement and puts the fee on the grantor. It also asks about farm valuation and any recoupment charge. A Sheriff Sales link sits on the Auditor's real estate page, and a 2026 pending special assessments file is posted there too.

Before signing a contract, ask the Treasurer for the balance and the Auditor about pending special assessments.

How are manufactured homes taxed and transferred in Wood County?

The Treasurer collects two kinds of property tax, real estate under R.C. 323.12 and manufactured homes under R.C. 4503.06, and both come due in February and July. A manufactured home is billed at the combined rate of the district where it sits, and a 1998 law moved its valuation toward market value, in the way real estate is assessed.

  • Conveyance fee on a mobile home: $1.00 per $1,000 of price, rounded up to the nearest thousand, plus $0.50 per title. No money changing hands means no fee.
  • Mobile home moving permit: $5.00, with a $100.00 fine for moving one without a permit.
  • Wood County's sales tax rate is 6.75 percent, as the Auditor's FAQ states.

More questions about Wood County, OH Property Tax Guide

Which months do Wood County property taxes fall due?

They fall due in February and July, on dates the Treasurer sets. Late payments cost 5 percent in the first 10 days and 10 percent afterward.

By how much did Wood County residential values change in 2026?

19 percent on average, says the Auditor's press release. Neighborhoods differ, and House Bills 920, 186 and 335 keep bills from rising as fast as values.

What is the last day for a Wood County Board of Revision complaint?

March 31 each year, listed as March 31, 2027 for tax year 2026 in the Auditor's update FAQ. The window opens January 1.

What does a Wood County deed cost at the Auditor?

$3.00 per $1,000 of price (rounded up to the nearest hundred) and $0.50 per parcel.

Which Wood County office answers tax questions?

Payments and bills go to the Treasurer at 419-354-9130. Value questions go to the Auditor's real estate office at 419-354-9173. A toll free line, 866-860-4140, serves both.
